items.title: Benchmark: support -c correctly
items.body:
give each client its own connection unless +m specified

readme.md documents `+m`/`-m` as "when enabled clients share a connection, otherwise each client has a separate connection". The classic (old-core) leg did not implement the second half: OldCoreBenchmarkBase built a single ConnectionMultiplexer in its constructor and `GetClient(int index)` ignored the index entirely, returning that one IDatabase to every worker. `Multiplexed` was never read on this leg at all -- `+m` parsed and then did nothing.

So `-c` was CONCURRENCY (in-flight requests pipelined onto one connection), not connection count, on the leg that ships. The fan-out above it was always correct: BenchmarkBase allocates ClientCount tasks and calls GetClient(i) per worker; only the worker-to-connection mapping collapsed.

A multiplexer is one connection per endpoint by design, so "a connection per client" means a multiplexer per client. Now builds `Multiplexed ? 1 : ClientCount` of them and maps worker i to `i % connectionCount`, so `+m` reproduces the previous behaviour exactly and is the only way to get it. NewCoreBenchmark already did this (`new(count: Multiplexed ? 1 : ClientCount)`); BridgeBenchmark shares this base and inherits the fix.

VERIFIED against a live server, sampling DURING the run from two independent vantage points -- the OS TCP table by owning pid, and the server's own CLIENT LIST:

  -c 1        OS 1,1,1,1     CLIENT LIST 1 (+ the cli itself)
  -c 8        OS 8,8,8,8     CLIENT LIST 8
  -c 50       OS 50,50,50,50 CLIENT LIST 50
  -c 50 +m    OS 1,1,1,1     CLIENT LIST 1

The `+m` cell is the discriminating one: without it, a fix that simply hard-wired N connections would pass just as happily. `--basic` also exercised (exit 0).

AND A BANNER THAT CANNOT AGREE WITH A FLAG THAT DID NOTHING. The per-test banner printed ", mux" whenever `+m` was passed -- including on the leg where it had no effect -- so it reported the FLAG, not the behaviour, and could not have caught this. `ConnectionCount` is virtual, defaulting to the intended count, and OldCoreBenchmarkBase overrides it with `_connectionMultiplexers.Length`: the number actually created. It is printed on the `### ... ###` announce line, which survives `-q` so a harness can gate on it, and in the per-test banner.

- [x] I fully and freely contribute this code in accordance with the [project license](../LICENSE) (and am legally able to do so)  
- [x] I take responsibility for this contribution's quality and correctness, including any portions produced with AI assistance (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md)).

items.title: Audit and correct Frodo reference benchmark fairness
items.body:
### Motivation

- Eliminate a fairness bias where the Original reference path performed an in-timed `memcpy` from `word_source` to `out` while SDA read directly from the word buffer. 
- Provide symmetric, pointer-based APIs and matched timed regions for Original and SDA full-sampler measurements so comparisons are apples-to-apples. 
- Restructure frontend/mapping/full-sampler microbenchmarks, timing, ordering, and CSV metadata so each scope is well-defined and reproducible.

### Description

- Add a symmetric Original API `frodo_original_sample_n_from_words(out, word_source, n, table)` and make `frodo_original_sample_n` delegate to it so `out==word_source` and `out!=word_source` are both supported without an in-timed `memcpy` (files: `online/frodo/frodo_sample_n.h`, `online/frodo/frodo_sample_n.c`).
- Replace the asymmetric dispatch that did `memcpy(out, word_source, ...)` with a call to the new `from_words` API so the Original timed path writes outputs directly in the same way SDA does (file: `online/frodo/frodo_sampler.c`).
- Introduce materialized frontend helpers `frodo_original_materialize_words` and `frodo_sda_materialize_words` and wire up a new `standalone-materialized-input-frontend` microbenchmark that produces `candidates[]` and `signs[]` (file: `online/frodo/frodo_sample_n_fast.c` and `benchmark/frodo/benchmark_frodo_breakdown.c`).
- Implement mapping-only timing that receives pre-materialized `candidates/signs` and only measures CDT lookup + sign application + equal-sized writes (file: `benchmark/frodo/benchmark_frodo_breakdown.c`).
- Preserve the existing branchless fused SDA production implementation and add parameter-specialized accept-before-map diagnostic implementations plus a dispatcher `frodo_sda_word_sample_n_accept_before_map` to compare behavior (files: `online/frodo/frodo_sample_n_fast.c` and per-param `frodo_sample_n_word*.c`).
- Replace ad-hoc `__rdtsc()` timing with a serialized timer helper `benchmark/common/bench_timer.h` that uses `lfence; rdtsc` / `rdtscp; lfence` on x86 and `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` elsewhere, and update benchmarks to use it (files: `benchmark/common/bench_timer.h`, modified benchmark sources).
- Add deterministic paired counterbalanced ordering (even reps: Original->SDA, odd reps: SDA->Original) and expand CSV provenance and accounting fields, plus update the shell runner to run sequential multi-process experiments and preserve raw rows (files: `benchmark/frodo/benchmark_frodo_breakdown.c`, `benchmark/scripts/run_frodo_benchmarks.sh`, `benchmark/README.md`).
- Add a correctness C test `test_fair_reference_paths` and other test coverage to validate aliasing, materialization, mapping/full equivalence, accept-before-map equivalence, and no-stats vs stats checksum agreement (file: `online/tests/test_frodo_sample_n.c`).

### Testing

- Release build and unit tests: ran `cmake -S . -B build-dev -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSDA_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON && cmake --build build-dev -j4` and `ctest --test-dir build-dev` with the available online tests, and all available tests passed (4/4 in this environment).
- Sanitizers: built `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DSDA_ENABLE_SANITIZERS=ON` and ran `ctest` under ASan/UBSan, and online tests passed (4/4) in the sanitizer build.
- Smoke benchmark: executed `FRODO_BENCH_REPETITIONS=1 FRODO_BENCH_WARMUP=0 FRODO_BENCH_SAMPLE_COUNT=256 build-dev/benchmark_frodo_breakdown` and validated CSV shape and fields, which succeeded.
- Full run: executed the updated runner `benchmark/scripts/run_frodo_benchmarks.sh` with `FRODO_BENCH_PROCESSES=5` and `FRODO_BENCH_REPETITIONS=31` (equal-size mode) and collected `build/benchmark-results/frodo/frodo_breakdown_raw.csv` and `frodo_sample_n_raw.csv`; the run completed and diagnostic comparisons between branchless and accept-before-map variants were produced.
- Notes: offline generation/tests that depend on `mpfr.h` were disabled by CMake in this environment because `mpfr.h` was not available; all online frozen-table tests and sanitizer tests executed here passed.

------

items.title: Simplify and rank benchmarks
items.body:
## What changed

- replace the Core/Extended split with one unified seven-challenge benchmark catalog
- remove the suite toggle, `u` hotkey, suite state, suite metadata, and difficulty suffixes from terminal task names
- rename the destructive full-catalog action to **Run All** and retain its exact turn count plus two-step confirmation
- anchor the previous/next selector buttons around a responsive cell sized for the longest challenge name, keeping render and click coordinates stable as selection changes
- add a sortable overall `RANK` column for each model/reasoning-effort combination
- add responsive, clickable Cost/Balanced/Speed weighting controls plus a `w` cycling hotkey; changing them recomputes existing ranks immediately
- compute ranking once per render and reuse it for display and Rank sorting; column sizing derives its maximum label from the distinct model/effort combinations without ranking the results
- move Easy/Moderate/Hard guidance into one README challenge table and document the ranking algorithm and measurement caveats
- bump the maintained minor version from `0.4.0` to `0.5.0`

## Ranking

Ranking aggregates every completed result row for a model/reasoning-effort combination. More passes dominate, followed by fewer failures. Within each identical pass/failure tier, Codexometer independently ranks total API-equivalent cost and total wall time, then combines the two ordinal ranks at 75/25 for Cost mode, 50/50 for Balanced, or 25/75 for Speed. This tier isolation prevents a failing combination from changing the efficiency trade-off between fully correct peers. Token usage remains visible but no longer affects rank. Missing or invalid cost receives the last cost-axis rank in its correctness tier rather than appearing artificially cheap; exact weighted-score ties share a rank, and ranks are provisional while results are still arriving.

The README now specifies the grouping key, aggregation and validation rules, competition ranking, exact formulas (`3C + T`, `C + T`, and `C + 3T`), final correctness-first comparison, missing-cost consequences, token independence, and provisional in-progress behavior.

## Why

The suite split consumed control space and added selection state without changing how an individual challenge was evaluated. A single catalog makes challenge navigation and full runs easier to understand. Compact terminal names reclaim room for ranking, while difficulty remains available where its meaning can be properly explained.

The anchored selector prevents the arrow controls and their mouse hit targets from shifting when task-name lengths differ.

## Validation

- `go test ./...`
- `go test -race -cover ./...`
- `go vet ./...`
- rebuilt the local binary and Darwin, Linux, and Windows distributions for amd64 and arm64
- regression coverage for unified ordering/names, exact Run All turn/task selection, stable selector coordinates and hit testing, correctness precedence and tier isolation, independent cost/time ranks, all three weighting modes, token independence, displayed-order hotkey cycling, immediate mouse/hotkey recomputation, responsive click surfaces, rank sorting, incomplete measurements, and exact ties
- regression coverage that Rank sorting reuses the supplied, mode-specific ranking map
- confirmed the rebuilt local binary reports `codexometer v0.5.0`

- **`netty-loom-spring-benchmarks` had no entry**, under a heading reading "all included in settings.gradle.kts". The benchmark entry links README.md's Benchmarks section instead of duplicating the run instructions.

## Why it mattered

items.title: chore(docs): remove the internal benchmarks and manuals, and correct the offload figures
items.body:
## Description

Most of what is removed here already has a counterpart upstream in the backend repo and will
arrive through the backend sync. What lives in this repo today is a second, hand-maintained
copy, so the two drift apart. Dropping them leaves a single source.

| This repo (removed) | backend counterpart |
|---|---|
| `backend/tests/benchmark_llama_server_prefill.py` | `tests/e2e/benchmark_llama_server_prefill.py` |
| `backend/tests/benchmark_offload_vram.py` | `tests/e2e/benchmark_offload_vram.py` |
| `docs/benchmarks.md` (zh) · `docs/benchmarks.en.md` | `docs/benchmarks.md` (en) |
| `docs/inference_manual.html` (zh) · `.en.html` | `docs/inference_manual.zh-TW.html` · `inference_manual.html` |
| `docs/finetune_manual.html` (zh) · `.en.html` | `docs/finetune_manual.zh-TW.html` · `finetune_manual.html` |
| `docs/site-map.html` | `docs/site-map.html` |

Note the language-suffix convention is **inverted** between the two repos: here the bare
`.html` / `.md` is the Traditional Chinese file and `.en` marks English, while upstream the
bare name is English and `.zh-TW` marks Chinese. The names collide but the languages do not
line up, so the sync needs to account for it rather than assume a same-name overwrite.

Three things have no upstream counterpart and are simply dropped:

- The two raw result files, `benchmark_llama_server_prefill_results.json` and
  `benchmark_offload_vram_results.json`. Upstream deliberately keeps benchmark output out of
  git (`chore(tests): keep the llama-server benchmark results out of git`) and writes it to a
  gitignored `tests/results/` instead. This repo now matches that.
- The three example configs: `examples/fine-tune_configs/Llama3.3-70B-finetune.json`,
  `examples/fine-tune_configs/qwen3.5-122b-lora-finetune.json`, and
  `examples/inference_configs/GPT-OSS-120B-demo-inference.json`. These were written here and
  exist nowhere else, so they go away rather than moving. The `examples/` directory is emptied
  and disappears.

**References updated:**

- `README.md` / `README.zh-TW.md` — drop the links and directory entries pointing at
  benchmarks, the site map, both HTML manuals, and `examples/`.
- `wiki/{en,zh}/comparisons/trusta-ast-vs-market-solutions.md`,
  `concepts/offload-mechanism.md`, `summary/trusta-ast-core-differentiation.md` — replace
  "see `benchmark_*.py` / reproduce it with that script / raw data in `*_results.json`" with
  "measured in-house". Those paths were already stale once upstream moved `tests/` to
  `tests/e2e/`; naming no path means a future upstream reorganisation cannot rot these pages
  again.

## Corrected figure

The published VRAM reduction was wrong and is corrected here, in
`wiki/{en,zh}/concepts/offload-mechanism.md` and
`wiki/{en,zh}/summary/trusta-ast-core-differentiation.md`.

The old figure compared whole-device VRAM against model weights. The device peak includes
whatever other processes were already holding, and the benchmark recorded that baseline
without ever subtracting it, so the reduction was understated. The backend PR fixes the
benchmark; this applies the same correction to what is already published:

    model peak = 13.39 - 1.65 = 11.74 GB
    reduction  = 1 - 11.74 / 27.508 = 57.3%        (was published as 51.3%)

This is **recomputed from the raw fields the original run recorded, not a new run**. The
full-GPU requirement, the pre-load baseline and the device peak were all captured correctly;
only the final arithmetic was wrong. The pages now state both numbers — the ~11.7 GB
attributable to the model and the ~13.4 GB the device actually peaked at — so the two are no
longer conflated.

**The tok/s figure is deliberately left at ~0.5 and flagged as pending.** The original run
stored a count of SSE chunks in the `completion_tokens` field, so the real token count was
never recorded and cannot be recovered. Confirming it needs the benchmark re-run against a GPU
with the weights available.

## Related Issues

<!-- e.g. Closes #123, Relates to #456 -->

## Checklist

- [x] The PR title follows [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/)
- [x] Commits follow Conventional Commits (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md))
- [ ] `pytest` passes locally — not run; no collected test was touched (`backend/pytest.ini`
      sets no `python_files`, so `benchmark_*.py` was never collected)
- [x] Tests were added or updated where relevant — n/a, deletions and documentation only
- [x] Documentation was updated where relevant (English and 繁體中文 where applicable)
- [x] I have read the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

## Notes for Reviewers

- **Merge order matters.** `benchmark_offload_vram.py` only exists upstream once the
  corresponding backend PR lands — it is added there in the same change that fixes the
  hard-coded paths. Merge that one first, or this table describes a file that is not there yet.
- The corrected reduction is arithmetic on already-recorded measurements, so it needs no GPU to
  verify: the three inputs are in the deleted `benchmark_offload_vram_results.json`, visible in
  this PR's diff.
- Every deleted filename was grepped across the repo; nothing links to them any more. The only
  remaining mentions are provenance notes in `wiki/{en,zh}/log.md` and
  `wiki/{en,zh}/sources/finetune_manual.md` ("Ingested `inference_manual.html`"), which record
  where the wiki content came from rather than linking to the file, so they were left as they
  are.
- The HTML manuals' content was already absorbed into `wiki/{en,zh}/sources/`; the wiki itself
  is untouched.

items.title: docs: sixty-six false statements, corrected against the tree
items.body:
# Sixty-six false statements in the documentation, corrected

A seven-group review swept every prose document against the code and the
tree. A second agent per group then tried to **refute** each finding
before it was trusted, because confident-but-wrong staleness claims have
cost this project time before. Nine were refuted and dropped. Seventy
survived, and every number in them was re-checked by hand before
anything was edited.

| Claim | Checked | Match |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 395 tests, not 388 | `pytest --collect-only` | yes |
| 449 evidence records, not 448 | `registry/evidence.json` | yes |
| 210 drill criteria over 199 graders | `drills --all`, `find` | yes |
| 14 tasks, 10 on a bare fixture | every `task.json` | yes |
| 10 items in the protected set, not 7 | `GOVERNANCE.md` | yes |

## The pattern

Prose written while something was true, left standing after it stopped
being true.

- **Nine documents said the drills have no graders.** They have 199.
- **Four routed a reader through the exception ledger or the RFC rung.**
  ADR-0004 withdrew both, and neither directory has ever existed.
- **Six said the checker refuses to merge a spike branch.**
  `grep -rni spike tools/ tests/ .github/` returns nothing at all.
- **The operators guide** sent Daniel to do three whole classes of
  action by hand that the validated adapter has resolved on his
  approval since 2026-08-03.

## Two that were dangerous rather than merely stale

`README.md`'s map sent a newcomer to `archive/` for the v1 tree, which
ADR-0003 moved to a tag. The one row meant to prevent a misroute caused
one.

`benchmark/README.md` documented preparation as `runner.py materialise`,
which places no process surface. Anyone following it prepares a run that
is neither v1 nor v2, which is the exact defect the 2026-08-08 review
existed to fix.

## What was not corrected, and why

**Four sit in the protected set**, two of which compile into every ORG
seed. `GOVERNANCE.md` requires an accepted ADR and Daniel.
[ADR-0005](org/decisions/ADR-0005-four-corrections-in-the-protected-set.md)
is **proposed, not accepted**, and names all four with their exact
replacements. It is the only ADR here I could not write as accepted,
because ADRs record `decided_by` and this one is not mine to decide.

**Three drill specs name paths that never existed**, including a tool
that has never been on any branch. The drill manifest says a spec never
changes without an ADR amendment, and two of the three are Wave A
oracles whose entire worth is that nobody has written to them since they
were frozen. Recorded in `benchmark/drills/README.md` instead of edited.
Nothing follows those paths at run time, so the drills run correctly and
only a reader is misled.

## Frozen and derived, handled properly

`benchmark/PROTOCOL.md` and `benchmark/README.md` are frozen. Six
corrections were made under ADR-0002 and recorded in
`FREEZE_MANIFEST.json` with the reason. No threshold, gate, session
count or scoring rule was touched.

Derived files were fixed **at the source**: `registry/coverage.json` for
the twenty capability rows, `org/tasks/T-0011.json` for the criteria
count, then regenerated. Nothing derived was hand-edited.

## Backing evidence

A deterministic sweep of all **1,148 path references across 377
documents**. Sixteen do not resolve, and every one is correct in
context: git tag references, the decisions that retired those paths, v1
surface descriptions inside the protocol, template placeholders, and the
drill paths now documented as never having existed.

## Verification

- `python -m tools.eos check` → 0 errors, 0 warnings
- `python -m pytest -q` → 395 passed
- `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` byte-identical
- Every derived view regenerates from its source

items.title: Map detector rules to CIS Benchmark controls
items.body:
## Summary

- Adds `src/cloud_hardening_lab/compliance/` — a `CIS_MAPPING_BY_RULE_ID` table plus `apply_cis_mapping()`, wired into `run_detectors()` alongside the existing scoring/remediation enrichment passes (same pattern as `remediation/guidance.py`).
- Adds four fields to `Finding`: `cis_control_id`, `cis_benchmark`, `cis_confidence`, `cis_note` (all `None`-defaulted, included in `to_dict()`), and a new "CIS Control" column in the Markdown report. JSON gets the fields automatically via `to_dict()`.
- Adds `docs/compliance-mapping.md`, documenting the CIS control ID, benchmark version, confidence level, and a plain-language caveat for every rule.
- Updates `docs/detection-rules.md`, `docs/sample-findings.md`, and README to reference the new mapping.

## CIS mappings and how they were verified

Every control ID below was checked against a live source before use (not from memory) — see `docs/compliance-mapping.md` for the full writeup.

| Rule | CIS Control | Benchmark | Confidence | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `IAM-001` | `1.16` | CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark **v1.4.0** | medium | Detector tests wildcard action alone; the CIS control is about the combined wildcard-action-and-resource condition. Also: this control was **removed in v3.0.0/v5.0.0** — v1.4.0 is the most recent version where it's still numbered. |
| `IAM-002` | `1.16` | v1.4.0 | medium | Same control, other half of the same condition (wildcard resource). |
| `IAM-003` | `2.1.4` | v3.0.0 | low | No CIS control found specifically for a generic "public principal" — mapped to the closest verified analog (S3 block-public-access), not a confirmed 1:1 match. |
| `EXP-001` | `2.1.4` | v3.0.0 | high | Direct match — S3 block-public-access. |
| `EXP-002` | `2.3.3` | v3.0.0 | high | Direct match — RDS `PubliclyAccessible` control, same field name our detector checks. |
| `NET-001` | `5.2` | v3.0.0 | medium | Control's literal test is `0.0.0.0/0`; our synthetic sample uses the reserved documentation CIDR `203.0.113.0/24` instead (per this repo's safety rules), so intent matches but the literal condition doesn't. |
| `K8S-001` | `5.2.2` | CIS Kubernetes Benchmark **v1.8.0** | medium | Confirmed via two independent mirrors of the official benchmark text. Number is version-sensitive — some tooling numbers the same recommendation `5.2.1` for older Kubernetes-aligned releases. |
| `STO-001`, `STO-002`, `K8S-002` | **Not covered** | — | — | No verified CIS control exists for generic storage encryption/versioning or container resource limits. Mapped to `None` with an explicit reason rather than a guessed number. |

Sources: [AWS's official CIS-to-Security-Hub control mapping page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/cis-aws-foundations-benchmark.html), [Tenable's CIS Kubernetes v1.8.0 audit mirror](https://www.tenable.com/audits/items/CIS_Kubernetes_v1.8.0_Level_1_Master.audit:a6b2d980c1bdf84ff67264aabac8dad5), [Aqua Security's CIS Kubernetes v1.23 compliance DB](https://avd.aquasec.com/compliance/kubernetes/cis-kubernetes-benchmarks-v1.23-1.23/5.2.2/).

## Other fixes bundled in

- **Editable install pointed at a stale duplicate clone.** `pip show` revealed this package was installed in editable mode from a different, older local clone under `Documents\Codex\...`, not this working directory. Reinstalled against the correct path — otherwise the new `compliance` package wouldn't have been importable and tests would have silently run against old code.
- Extended the docs/source safety checks (`scripts/check-docs.py` and `tests/test_source_and_sample_safety.py`) to allow the specific external citation domains (`docs.aws.amazon.com`, `www.tenable.com`, `avd.aquasec.com`) and the `0.0.0.0` placeholder address that the new compliance docs legitimately reference, without loosening the checks for anything else.

## Test plan

- [x] `python -m pytest --cov=cloud_hardening_lab --cov-report=term-missing --cov-fail-under=90` — 113 passed, 97.97% coverage
- [x] `python -m ruff check .` — all checks passed
- [x] `python -m ruff format --check .` — 53 files already formatted
- [x] `python scripts/check-docs.py` — passed
- [x] New `tests/test_cis_mapping.py` — mapping table completeness, per-category sample runs, JSON/Markdown report field checks
- [x] CLI smoke (`--help`, `scan --fail-on high`) — clean
- [x] Regenerated `reports/examples/cloud_hardening_report.{md,json}` from the synthetic samples

items.title: docs(benchmarks): document benchmark lifecycle and release 1.11
items.body:

items.title: Take weavatrix-edit 0.1.6, keep the capturing decode, correct published claims
items.body:
## Summary

Takes `weavatrix-edit` 0.1.6 and **keeps the capturing decode**, then corrects the published claims that an adversarial review found stale or overstated.

## Why no call site switched to `DeclaredEditPlan`

Upstream 0.1.6 added a declared-only decode that is roughly twice as fast on plans carrying extensions. This crate cannot use it, and the reason is stronger than evidence loss:

- Plan annotations live entirely in undeclared members. `EDIT_PLAN_FIELDS` has 4 members; every v1 annotation this crate writes is undeclared.
- `src/extension.rs` walks every extension map through `JsonBudget` and performs the reserved-key check. On an empty map both are no-ops.

So a declared-only decode here is a **validation bypass**, not an optimization: `tests/declared_decode.rs` shows a 5,000-node annotation blob rejected with `EvidenceTooLarge` after a capturing decode and passing validation after a declared-only decode of identical bytes.

For the benchmark, `parse_validate` is paired against `JSON.parse`, which has no declared-only mode, and the workloads carry undeclared members at all three levels — switching would delete measured work rather than perform it faster.

## Corrections

| Where | Was | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `README.md` | "a model that drops them decodes in 300 µs where the eager one takes 1,284 µs" | roughly twice as fast; upstream retracted the 1,284 figure as a harness-local model (the shipped envelope measured ~680 in the same run) |
| `README.md` | "lazy extension capture is the open optimization" | it shipped as `DeclaredEditPlan` and is deliberately declined here, with the reason |
| `README.md` | performance table presented as current | qualified: measured against `weavatrix-edit` 0.1.5, whose envelope codecs were since rewritten inside the timed region |
| `docs/benchmarks/publication-2026-08-03.md` | class table said `weavatrix-edit@0.1.3`, footer said `0.1.5` | inline correction note; the frozen artifact is otherwise untouched |
| `tools/benchmarks/report.mjs` | `canonicalize@3.0.0` hardcoded | read from the run, like the other compared packages |
| `tools/benchmarks/test/report.test.mjs` | guarded three packages | guards the fingerprint oracle too, which was the remaining literal |

## Gates

`cargo fmt`, `clippy --locked --all-targets --all-features -D warnings`, `cargo test --locked --all-features`, Rust 1.88 `--locked`, `rustdoc -D warnings`, and `npm test` (8/8) all pass.

A publication rerun on a frozen tree is still owed before the README table can be replaced; this PR does not claim new numbers.

items.title: benchmarks: the paper was understating mapquik threefold
items.body:
Found while building the corpus on galaxy. **The paper's comparison table has been understating mapquik by a factor of three.**

mapquik counts newlines as bases, so `suite.toml` overrides its reference with a one-line FASTA. That was found, documented at length, and the corpus was re-run with the corrected reference on 2026-07-31 at 14:44. `--export` was never run afterwards, so the committed manifest kept the 03:50 measurement made against the *wrapped* reference:

| | mapped | reference used |
|---|---:|---|
| committed manifest | 48 913 | `.../hs1.fa` |
| actual cache | **148 225** | `.../REF-HS1.oneline.fa` |

`paper.py` reads the committed manifest, so the table reported mapquik mapping **33%** of the reads when it maps **99.2%**. All four of its benchmarks were wrong the same way, and the error ran in one direction: it understated another group's tool in the table where we compare ourselves against it.

Corrected by re-exporting — B01–B04 become 148 225 / 124 221 / 239 539 / 2 394 360, and peak RSS drops from ~19.4 GB to ~18.1 GB. Winnowmap2's numbers were already right.

## Why nothing caught it

Every other generated artifact here has a `--check` that fails when it drifts from its source: RESULTS.md, README.md, the charts, the paper artifacts, the cross-arch document. This manifest had none — it's generated from a host-local corpus rather than from a result set, so it sat outside the entire checking scheme.

It has one now. `reference_mappers.py --check` compares the committed manifest against the host's cache and fails on any disagreement; `promote.py` runs it.

**Deliberately not in CI.** GitHub runners have no corpus, so there it could only report that it cannot check — and a step that structurally cannot fail reads like verification while providing none. Same reasoning that makes `validate_suite.py` treat a missing corpus as a note rather than an error.

## Staleness no longer keys on absolute paths

A second fault, which camouflaged the first. The cache key includes the full command line, and the command line embeds input paths — so when the datasets moved behind `benchmarks/data/files/`, all nine entries went stale. That's 3.5 hours of Winnowmap2 invalidated by nothing about the data. Worse, uniform staleness is indistinguishable from the real drift above.

The key already carries what determines a result: mapper version, dataset ids, and each input's `(bytes, records, bases)`. Paths aren't part of that. Comparing basenames keeps every genuine change detectable — `hs1.fa` and `REF-HS1.oneline.fa` are still different, so **the very bug above would still be caught** — while surviving a move of the corpus root. All nine entries read `cached` again.

Full cheap tier green, plus `reference_mappers.py --check` passing on a2.

Promotes the preview line to **v2.7.0-preview**: 47 commits since the v2.6.0-preview tag, stamped and documented. The release entry and the readme land in this PR; the tag follows the merge.

## What the release is

**The dispatch contract, pinned and then corrected.** A contract suite went in first — public surface only, both registration axes, with a committed lane map that turns "the same behavior arrived through a different path" into a reviewable diff — and grew from 83 scenarios to 193. What it pinned made four corrections safe to land: the abort semantics, one value for a resultless pipeline, covariant main handlers, and one exception type for "nothing will handle this". Exception interceptors gained a typed form, and the registration window is now stated rather than implied.

Full detail in the CHANGELOG entry; the three source-breaking changes are listed under its Notes.

- **readme.md** — covariant main-handler matching, typed exception interceptors and abort semantics join *Pipeline control*; the registration window joins *Dispatch architecture*; `RegisterFromAssembly` is marked as on its way out; the benchmark table is re-measured on this tree today.

Contract suite 193/193 on both TFMs, full solution green, lane map re-captured at every phase that moved one. The 2026-08-11 hardware-counter capture (elevated, single-core) reports ~0 cache misses and ~0 branch mispredictions on every lane.

## Intent The developer asked for a thorough code review of the Switchyard repository (as of main) covering CLAUDE.md, README, design docs, and ADRs, with the explicit constraint that deliberately deferred features (Prometheus/OTel, CLI, second scheduling policy, real Docker executor benchmark, aging/warmth-decay, merge queue/autoscaler/remote cache) must not be flagged as defects. Priorities, in order: (1) find other reachable invariant-violating paths beyond the two bugs already found this session (FIFO head-of-line starvation, capacity over-count under bin-packing), focusing on the non-negotiable invariants listed in CLAUDE.md; (2) verify the policy/scheduler purity and determinism contract (no wall-clock, I/O, unseeded randomness, or raw map iteration); (3) confirm the scheduler core stays properly agnostic of Docker/simulation backends via the Clock/Executor/Policy seam; (4) identify test-coverage gaps that hide invariant violations, not just low coverage percentage; (5) surface any other correctness bugs in scheduler/executor/simulation/bench code. The developer required the review to be read-only (no code changes), with each finding given a severity, exact file:line, concrete reproduction/reasoning, and a note on whether an existing test catches it, keeping style/maintainability feedback brief and separate from genuine defects so they can personally triage which findings to act on. ## What Changed - Reworded seven README claims that described unbuilt or partially-built capabilities as present-tense features — real Docker execution, fault tolerance/failure injection, lease fencing, in-flight cancellation, retries, Prometheus/OTel metrics, and benchmark warm-up discard — now marked `(planned)` or narrowed to what actually exists (e.g. only `FakeExecutor` today). - Corrected two overstated claims: simulator scale ("hundreds of thousands of jobs" → "tens to thousands today," blocked on the known O(N²) snapshot cost) and invariant checking ("checked on every run" → narrowed to the capacity and work-conservation checkers that are actually implemented), each cross-referenced to its tracked known-issue (F1, F5, F8, F10, F15). - Rewrote the Failure semantics section to frame lease-based recovery as intended design rather than working behavior, and updated the ADR count to reflect the 4 ADRs actually written. - Logged the README-accuracy audit and the corrections applied in `docs/build-log.md`. ## Risk Assessment ✅ Low: Docs-only change (README.md and build-log.md) that corrects overstated claims to match verified known-issues (F1, F5, F6, F8, F10, F15); items.title: docs: correct drifted benchmark prose, format version, and API signatures
items.body:
Fixes every confirmed docs drift in #296, #297 and #298. Each claim below was re-verified against the source or the benchmark JSONs in this tree rather than taken from the issue text — which matters, because **the ARM numbers in #298 are themselves already stale**: the c4a Axion re-baseline (#290, merged in `44571a3`) moved them again after the issue was filed.

## ARM speed prose (#298)

Recomputed from `benchmarks/results/speed_d*_arm_*.json` as `faiss/tq − 1`:

| cell | mt | st |
|---|---|---|
| d1536 2-bit | +30.7% | +31.1% |
| d1536 4-bit | +21.2% | +23.6% |
| d3072 2-bit | +19.4% | +20.6% |
| d3072 4-bit | +20.8% | +23.6% |

True span is **19–31%**. `README.md:19` said "10–19%" and `README.md:155` said "16–24%" — two different wrong ranges, both now 19–31%.

Checked and left alone because they are exactly right against the current JSONs: the x86 speed prose (`README.md:163` — 4-bit +5.0/+2.5/+2.4/+0.0%, 2-bit −7.8/−2.8/−3.0/−5.8%, d3072 4-bit mt ties) and all recall prose (`README.md:135` — d1536/d3072 R@1 gaps span 0.2–1.9pp; GloVe 4-bit +0.88pp; GloVe 2-bit −0.06pp, "within 0.1 points").

Note this PR does **not** address the other half of #312: the recall JSONs themselves predate the v5 rotation change, so the prose is now consistent with files that need regenerating on the official benchmark hosts. That rerun is left for @RyanCodrai.

## Format version and API signatures (#297)

- `docs/api.md:160,188` — both format diagrams showed `version u8 = 4`; `io.rs:64,66` define `TV_VERSION`/`TVIM_VERSION` as **6**. A reader parsing `.tv` from the diagram would reject valid files. Now 6.
- `docs/api.md:48,114` — method tables listed `write(path)`; the real signature is `write(path, *, durable=True)` on both classes (`turbovec-python/src/lib.rs:459,888`). `grep -rn durable docs/ README.md` previously returned zero hits for a shipped public parameter. Both rows now carry the signature and a one-line description of what `durable=False` trades away.
- `README.md:83` — said allowlist output length is `min(k, len(allowed))`; `id_map.rs:259-265` deduplicates the allowlist, so it is `min(k, n_allowed)` over *distinct* ids. `docs/api.md:143` already said this correctly; the README now matches.
- Cosmetic docstrings visible in `help()`: `IdMapIndex.write` had two concatenated intro sentences from a merge, and `IdMapIndex.load` leaked rustdoc link syntax (``[`IdMapIndex.write`]``). Both cleaned.

## agno integration docs (#296)

- `docs/integrations/agno.md:113` claimed `delete()` is an "alias for drop(), returns True". `agno.py:272-276` returns `False` and deletes nothing (deliberate — it matches LanceDb; destruction goes through `drop()`). The doc page was the wrong one, so it now says so.
- `agno.md:151` implied the async paths fall back for a sync-only embedder. They do not: the `hasattr` guard at `agno.py:846` never fires because `agno.knowledge.embedder.base.Embedder` always defines `async_get_embedding` (its body raises `NotImplementedError`). Reworded to describe the real behaviour.

## Verification

Docs-only plus two Rust docstrings; `cargo check -p turbovec-python` clean. Percentages recomputed directly from the committed JSONs; every source claim quoted above was read in this tree.

items.body:
This pull request introduces several improvements to how HirayaCoder handles file and directory operations, tool usage, and benchmarking. The main changes include smarter handling of shell commands that overlap with existing tools, improved refusal messages, stricter planning to avoid unachievable steps, and the addition of a build-from-scratch benchmark. Documentation has also been updated to clarify requirements and protocols.

**Tool Handling and Refusals:**

* [`app/agent/tools/runScript.js`](diffhunk://#diff-936785704922fe2c7cfbe2ebf23db4b0b4e40ed0a819c4987fd20b6f40c1885cR25-R93): Shell commands that duplicate existing HirayaCoder tools (e.g., `ls`, `cat`, `rm`, `mkdir`) are now mapped to the appropriate tool, and refusal messages explicitly name the tool to use instead. For `mkdir`, the agent is told that no directory creation is needed because `write_file` handles it. This prevents repeated, unhelpful refusals and guides the model to the correct action. [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-936785704922fe2c7cfbe2ebf23db4b0b4e40ed0a819c4987fd20b6f40c1885cR25-R93) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-936785704922fe2c7cfbe2ebf23db4b0b4e40ed0a819c4987fd20b6f40c1885cR109-R126) [[3]](diffhunk://#diff-936785704922fe2c7cfbe2ebf23db4b0b4e40ed0a819c4987fd20b6f40c1885cL117-R195) [[4]](diffhunk://#diff-936785704922fe2c7cfbe2ebf23db4b0b4e40ed0a819c4987fd20b6f40c1885cR233-R234)

* [`app/agent/toolRegistry.js`](diffhunk://#diff-7c1c723687d31afb7ab0cacd0702bc16e77365836bb4d9d33eb299d5e1a0e805L134-R137): The description for `run_script` now clarifies that it is for build tooling, not file or folder manipulation, and lists which commands should be replaced by tools.

**Planning Improvements:**

Documentation is updated with requirements (including allow-listed toolchains), benchmark protocols, and the rationale for tool restrictions. [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-06572a96a58dc510037d5efa622f9bec8519bc1beab13c9f251e97e657a9d4edR8-R77) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-eca12c0a30e25b4b46522ebf89465a03ba72a03f540796c979137931d8f92055R108-R121) [[3]](diffhunk://#diff-b335630551682c19a781afebcf4d07bf978fb1f8ac04c6bf87428ed5106870f5R123-R130) [[4]](diffhunk://#diff-b335630551682c19a781afebcf4d07bf978fb1f8ac04c6bf87428ed5106870f5R160-R209)

items.title: Fix lucky imaging pipeline quality: warping sign, flow scale, reference selection, and add realistic 30-min scenario
items.body:
Four bugs were degrading output quality, and the README lacked a realistic end-to-end example showing what a full 30-minute planetary observation produces.

## Bug fixes

### Critical: warping direction was inverted
`revert_deformation` was **adding** the flow instead of subtracting it — doubling the distortion rather than cancelling it.
```python
# Before (wrong — amplifies distortion)
map_x = x_coords + flow[:, :, 0]
# After (correct — inverts the displacement)
map_x = x_coords - flow[:, :, 0]
```

### Turbulence amplitude too large for DIS (`ELASTIC_ALPHA` 400 → 80)
`alpha=400` produced ~20 px RMS displacements. DIS optical flow loses accuracy beyond ~8 px; reducing to 80 keeps the synthetic turbulence in the regime where the algorithm can actually recover the flow.

### Reference frame selected by sharpness only
A frame can be sharp yet highly deformed (a single lucky turbulence pattern). `find_reference_frame` now combines two normalised metrics:
- **Laplacian variance** (sharpness)
- **Geometric stability** — inverse mean absolute deviation from the temporal mean (proximity to the average geometry)

### DIS preset upgraded (`MEDIUM` → `FAST`)
`PRESET_FAST` gives meaningfully higher flow accuracy for this use-case at comparable speed.

## Realistic 30-minute observation scenario

Added `run_realistic_observation()` to `benchmark.py` (invoked via `--realistic`), modelling a 30 fps × 30 min session with top-10% frame selection (~5,400 usable frames; demo uses 500 for speed). Generates separate README assets:

- `docs/assets/comparison_strip_realistic.png`
- `docs/assets/stacking_convergence_realistic.gif`

```bash
python benchmark.py --realistic
# Full-scale run:
REALISTIC_FRAMES=5400 python benchmark.py --realistic
```

The README now includes a dedicated section with the visual comparison, convergence animation, and measured metrics (PSNR/SSIM) for the 500-frame stack, plus an explanation of why individual corrected frames score lower than the stack (flow noise cancels when averaged; geometry coherence does not).

> 메일은 §2.1b를 인용)... 원래 acceptance는 철회한다 — 해당 결함은 코드 수정
> (#75/#79)으로 이미 해소됐고 그 증거가 wiki1m canonical 산출물이다. 결함 CSV는
> 재측정 대상이 아니라 은퇴 대상이다."

The docs described the project's dataset hierarchy backwards relative to
actual practice: `BENCHMARK.md` declared Cohere 1M×1024 "Primary dataset" and
"canonical" (§2.1a) while carrying a known `index_bytes=0` defect, and
demoted the wiki_all_1M cross-machine reproduction (§2.1b) — the dataset
NVIDIA's 2026-07-24 email and #98 actually cite — to a "reproduction"
footnote.

## Changes (3 commits, split by intent)

1. **Artifact rename + ledger** — `bench/results/pg_cuvsbench_1m.csv` →
   `pg_cuvsbench_1m_legacy.csv` (`git mv`); `bench/results/README.md` ledger
   row updated to `legacy` status with a one-line defect note (was a 17-line
   block); wording states the fix (#75/#79) and canonical wiki_all_1M rows
   as the corrected evidence.
2. **BENCHMARK.md / README.md hierarchy** — §0 "Primary dataset" → wiki_all_1M
   (Cohere relabeled "Legacy dataset"); §2.1a heading/framing: canonical →
   "legacy dataset (Cohere)", scoped as "canonical within the Cohere lineage"
   where that's still accurate (it's the fix lineage for the k-wiring/
   VRAM-accounting defects); §2.1b promoted to canonical. README's benchmark
   section now leads with the wiki_all_1M ~5.4× citation (existing §2.1b
   number, not a new measurement) and demotes the Cohere table to a labeled
   legacy comparison — its own ratios (~4.5× search, ~2× build) are **not
   deleted**, just relabeled per dataset.
3. **Reference sweep** — every live doc naming the old filename or implying
   Cohere-as-primary: `ROADMAP.md` (#92 release-readiness row rewritten for
   the redefined scope; the dated ADR-080 completion entry gets its filename
   updated in place, narrative untouched), `bench/cuvs_bench_backend/README.md`
   + `run_pg_cuvsbench.py` (usage examples), `design/benchmarks/crossover-methodology.md`
   (filename + rename pointer in an existing baseline-reconciliation note).

## What I deliberately did NOT touch

- **`design/specs/phase-record.md:1201`** — `docs/doc-map.md` states it is
  frozen history ("Do not reopen ... it is frozen history"). Left as-is; it
  still names the old filename in a historical evidence line, which is
  accurate as written (it was true at the time).
- **`design/decisions.md` ADR-080 body** (evidence table, numbers, `데이터
  정합성 정정` note) — append-only per `docs/doc-map.md`. Added a short dated
  addendum after the existing block, matching the doc's own precedent for
  self-correction notes (the existing 정정 note at the same ADR), recording
  the hierarchy change without rewriting the original evidence.
- **Ratio claims** (~4.5×/~5× search, ~2× build) — same-run comparisons,
  kept as valid; only the primary/canonical *dataset* label moved.

## Investigation note: `pg_cuvsbench_1m_guarded.csv`

The issue mentioned a "ledger-unregistered byte-identical duplicate"
`pg_cuvsbench_1m_guarded.csv`. I confirmed it is **byte-identical** to the
original `pg_cuvsbench_1m.csv` (`diff` clean), but it is **not tracked by
git anywhere in history** on any branch — it exists only as an untracked
local file in one contributor's working directory. There is nothing to
rename/remove in this repo; no action taken here. Worth a heads-up to
whoever has that local file, but out of scope for this PR.

## Verification

- `bash scripts/docs-contract-check.sh` → `[OK] documentation contract
  checks passed` (run after every commit).
- No `src/` changes, no code behavior changes (the two `.py` docstring/
  comment edits are example `--out` paths only).
- `grep -rn "pg_cuvsbench_1m\.csv"` (excluding `_legacy`) across the repo
  now only matches `design/specs/phase-record.md` (frozen) and the original
  evidence block inside `design/decisions.md`'s ADR-080 (intentionally
  preserved, append-only).

## Test plan

- [x] `scripts/docs-contract-check.sh` passes
- [x] All new/changed relative links point at files that exist
      (`pg_cuvsbench_1m_legacy.csv`, `pg_cuvsbench_wiki1m.csv`,
      `pg_cuvsbench_wiki1m_brev.csv`)
- [ ] CI green (Tier-1) — watching after push

Relates to #92 (redefined scope). This PR intentionally does **not** close the issue,
per the task instructions; leaving that to the issue owner to confirm intent
was fully captured.

items.title: docs(examples): add the visualization and benchmarking notebooks
items.body: `examples/README.md` had advertised both notebooks — and two scripts — none of which existed. The notebooks now exist, committed **with their executed outputs** so they render on GitHub without being run. ## The notebooks **`visualization.ipynb`** — training history shown with its stochastic noise rather than smoothed, solution evolution against the exact solution, a space–time error heat map, an interactive Plotly time slider, and `residual="rk"` vs `residual="interpolant"` on one seed. **`benchmarking.ipynb`** — cost per step split into forward and backward, scaling in slabs and spatial batch, autograd-graph memory, a CPU/GPU (or thread-count) comparison, and the accuracy-per-unit-cost study: all three tableaux are 2-stage yet recover classical orders 4, 3 and 2. It reproduces **3.97 / 2.97 / 1.97** through the shipped code path. Every figure and number was produced by executing the notebook against the current code. ## Executing them contradicted my own prose — twice Both times the text was wrong, not the code. **1. "Error is smallest at `t=0`, where the IC penalty pins the solution."** It isn't: 2.9e-2 at `t=0` against 1.6e-2 at `t=0.1`. The real explanation is better — absolute error falls because the *solution* decays by `exp(-π²T) ≈ 0.37`, while relative error grows. And the IC penalty is an H¹ **seminorm**: it matches `∂ₓu`, not values, so it never pinned `u(·,0)` pointwise at all. **2. "Cost is flat across tableaux."** Contradicted by `gauss2` reading 2118ms against ~900ms elsewhere. That was warm-up pollution, so I changed the **harness**, not the sentence: a throwaway measurement first, and the **minimum** of repeats rather than the median — timing noise is strictly additive, so the fastest run is the least contaminated estimate. | | before | after | | --- | --- | --- | | `gauss2` rk | 2118 ms | 124 ms | | `radau2` rk | 893 ms | 132 ms | | `lobatto2` interpolant | 986 ms | 116 ms | The original figures were almost entirely noise. The corrected data supports the weaker *true* claim: `rk` costs modestly more (124/132/147ms vs 94/99/116ms) because it evaluates at both slab endpoints. ## A guard so this can't regress `tests/test_notebooks.py` (5 tests) asserts the notebooks parse, store **no error outputs**, carry execution counts and rendered figures, and don't shim `sys.path`. It reads them as plain JSON, so it runs in CI where the optional `examples` group isn't installed. It caught an unexecuted notebook on its very first run. ## Documentation corrected rather than extended - Removed a **malformed YAML front-matter block** at the top of `examples/README.md`, which rendered as raw text and duplicated example 02's description - Replaced a **fabricated** convergence table (rates 0.91 / 0.92 / 0.92) with measured consistency orders, explicitly labelled as consistency rather than trained-model results - `--save-plots`, `--output-dir`, `--export-csv` belonged to a script that doesn't exist and are gone (`--save-model` is real and stayed) - `03_custom_operator.py` and `04_convergence_study.py` are labelled **not yet written** instead of advertised as available ## Ruff config `.ruff.toml` gains `"examples/notebooks/*.ipynb" = ["T201", "C408"]` — `print` is how a notebook reports results, and `dict(...)` is the idiom throughout Plotly's own docs. This is not a blanket ignore: the one genuine lint (`B905`, unguarded `zip`) was fixed in the source and the notebook re-executed. ## Side effect This makes the optional `examples` dependency group honest — `jupyter`, `matplotlib` and `plotly` were declared but entirely unused, which is what generated most of the Dependabot advisories cleared in #3. Notebooks add ~620 KiB total. Test suite 41 → 50. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Adds two executed example notebooks and tests that verify they run cleanly and include outputs. Cleans up example docs and adjusts lint rules for notebooks. - **New Features** - Added `examples/notebooks/visualization.ipynb` with training history, exact-solution comparisons, space–time error map, Plotly time slider, and `residual="rk"` vs `"interpolant"`. Committed with outputs for GitHub rendering. - Added `examples/notebooks/benchmarking.ipynb` with cost per step (forward/backward), scaling, memory, CPU/GPU or thread sweep, and measured consistency orders (4/3/2). Committed with outputs. - Added `tests/test_notebooks.py` to assert notebooks parse, have no error outputs, were executed (execution counts and figures), and import the installed package (no `sys.path` shims). - **Bug Fixes** - Corrected `examples/README.md`: removed malformed YAML, replaced fabricated convergence table with measured consistency orders, removed nonexistent flags, and marked planned scripts as not yet written. Linked notebooks and added run instructions in `README.md`. Updated `CHANGELOG.md`. - Updated `.ruff.toml` to ignore `T201` and `C408` for `examples/notebooks/*.ipynb` so notebooks lint without suppressing real issues elsewhere. Written for commit aba52f46900427c9d8ef5ecdd462660fca984f19. Summary will update on new commits.

items.title: chore(benchmarks): build benchmarks in the release preset, fix and document the harness
items.body:
## Summary

Three related changes that make the benchmark suite buildable, correct, and documented.

**1. `fix(benchmarks)` — KLU/SuperLU scoreboards did not compile.**
`bench_klu.cpp` and `bench_superlu.cpp` reached for `blk.L` / `blk.U` on `lu_numeric`, but those members are private (`L_` / `U_`, `sparse_lu.hpp:145-146`). Nothing caught it because `MTL5_BUILD_BENCHMARKS` defaults to `OFF` and no preset turned it on, so the files had not been compiled since `lu_numeric` was encapsulated. Switched to the public `factorL()` / `factorU()` accessors (`sparse_lu.hpp:75-76`), which return the same `const csc_matrix&` — fill accounting is unchanged.

**2. `chore(build)` — the release preset built nothing.**
It set `MTL5_BUILD_TESTS=OFF` and `MTL5_BUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF`, and benchmarks default off, leaving a configured tree with zero buildable targets (the only target, `mtl5`, is an `INTERFACE` header-only library). `MTL5_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON` now yields `bench_all`, `bench_sparse`, `bench_klu`, `bench_superlu` in their native-only configuration. **No CI workflow uses this preset**, so no CI surface changes.

**3. `docs(benchmarks)` — README refreshed and published.**
The README documented only `bench_all` and had drifted from the code:

- Layout listed none of the three sparse binaries, neither scaling driver, nor `analyze_scaling.py` / the `fetch_*.sh` downloaders.
- The suite list predated #227 — `l2` is `gemv+ger+symv+trmv+trsv`, `l3` is `gemm+trmm+trsm+symm+syrk+syr2k`, plus `gemm-rect` and `ewise`.
- "BLAS routine coverage" still listed the entire L2/L3 core as unimplemented; #227 closed that.

All three synced against `bench_all.cpp` and `runner.hpp`, plus new sections on the sparse scoreboards, the #297 scaling driver, and how concurrency is selected — including the trap that the threaded GEMM/GEMV paths sit behind `#ifdef MTL5_NATIVE_FAST_GEMM` (`mult.hpp:217-258`), so a plain build shows no dense scaling however `MTL5_NUM_THREADS` is set.

It is published at `/mtl5/benchmarks/` through `ROOT_FILE_MAP`, which resolves against the repo root — the README stays next to the code it documents instead of moving into `docs/`. `src/content/docs/` remains 100% generated.

## Testing

- `cmake --preset release && cmake --build build-release -j$(nproc)` — all four benchmark targets build clean; both previously-broken ones now compile and link.
- `bench_klu` runs and prints its scoreboard header, correctly reporting that external KLU is not linked in this configuration. Not a full benchmark sweep.
- `npm run build` in `docs-site/` — 41 pages (was 40); `/mtl5/benchmarks/` renders with its 4 tables, working in-page anchors, and the new "Benchmarking" sidebar entry; Pagefind indexed it.
- Verified against a running `npm run dev`: `/mtl5/benchmarks/` returns 200.

## Notes

- `benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt:37` claims `bench_sparse` runs "under `run_scaling.sh` with `SUITE=sparse-solve`"; no such variable exists — `run_scaling_297.sh:88` drives it as its `sparse` family via `--sizes`. The README describes actual behavior; the stale comment is left for a follow-up.
- A tracking issue follows for reporting i7-12700K results as a benchmark landing page plus linked result pages.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.title: [bench-account-roster] Model both accounts in the guard benchmark
items.body:
## Motivation

Codex raised this on #49 and it went in unaddressed. The guard benchmark's `gh`
stub returned a roster holding one account, `bench-active`, while the
wrong-account fixture declared `someone-else`. So the case measured "the
expected account is not authenticated at all", not the scenario the arm claims
to measure — two accounts authenticated, and the guard has to pick the active
one.

With a one-entry roster, `map(select(.active)) | .[0]` and a bare `.[0]` return
the same login. The arm scored `ghaccount 6/6` whether the guard was right or
had regressed to the first entry.

The guard itself is correct and stays correct — `gh-account-guard.sh:153`
selects on `.active`, and `verify-gh-account-guard.sh` already parameterises the
roster through `STUB_GH_ROSTER`. What was wrong is that the *published number*
did not exercise the property it was being read as evidence for.

## Changes

- `scripts/bench-guards.sh` — the stub roster now carries both accounts, with
  `someone-else` first and without the active flag. The ordering is the
  measurement: first-entry selection has to produce a visibly different result

## Verification

`make verify`, `make verify BASH=/bin/bash` (3.2.57) and `make verify-all` all
exit 0.

`make bench` with the corrected roster — published numbers unchanged, because
the guard was already doing the right thing:

    harness    33 / 35  (94%)      2 / 30  (7%)
    ghaccount   6 / 6  (100%)

Then the detector itself was checked, since a fixture that cannot fail is worth
nothing. Mutating the guard's selector to `.[0].login` (asserting first that the
mutation actually applied, via `cmp`):

    ghaccount        6 / 6  ->  0 / 6
    incidents      33 / 35  -> 27 / 35
    false positives 2 / 30  ->  4 / 30

It moves in both directions: the regressed guard stops blocking the wrong
account, and starts blocking legitimate pushes from the right one. The guard was
restored from git and `git status` shows only the benchmark script changed.

## Notes

No published figure moves, so `docs/agent-layer.md` §4 needs no edit — its
category line already reads `ghaccount 6/6` and still does.

This is the second of two findings from earlier reviews that were never applied.
The other one is stale percentages in the English README and `agent-layer.md`
(`8%` and `93%` where the benchmark prints `7%` and `94%`); it is a documentation
change with no code in it and goes in its own PR.

items.title: perf: add fragment links to benchmark corpus generator (#357)
items.body:
## PERF-035: add fragment links to the benchmark corpus generator Closes #357 ### What The testdata-generator previously emitted only plain `[[entity]]` wiki-links, so heading-harvest (and follow-on perf work like PERF-032's dirty-expansion measurement) could not be benchmarked without hand-editing the corpus. This adds `--fragment-links N`: - Emits N deterministic `[[entity#overview]]` wiki fragment links on every generated page (targets are the next N generation positions, wrapping, never self — same selection as `--dense-links`). - `overview` is a real heading on every generated page (`## Overview`), so the tree builds clean and every referenced page becomes a heading-harvest fragment target. - Both link modes compose; with neither set, corpus output is byte-identical to previous versions (verified by the determinism unit tests, which now cover the fragment mode too). ### Verification - `zig test tools/testdata-generator/main.zig` — 9/9 pass, including new parse, content, and determinism coverage for `--fragment-links`. - End-to-end: `--pages=200 --fragment-links=8` corpus builds clean with Boris (exit 0), `heading_harvest` does real work (680 ms at 200 pages), and fragment hrefs land in output (`sections/section-0000.html#overview`). - `zig build test` — full suite green. - Default corpus bytes unchanged, so the pinned `benchmark-1k` baseline is untouched. ### Changelog - `docs/changelog.d/357-benchmark-corpus-fragment-links.md`

Greptile Summary

The PR adds deterministic fragment-link generation to the benchmark corpus so heading harvesting can be measured without modifying generated data manually. - Adds parsing, help text, generation, and reporting for `--fragment-links N`. - Emits links to the next N generated pages while wrapping, excluding self-links, and clamping to the available page count. - Adds fragment-mode content and determinism tests plus README and changelog documentation.

Confidence Score: 5/5

The PR appears safe to merge with no actionable correctness, security, or repository-rule issues identified. Fragment targets map to existing generated pages, exclude their source page, and use an `overview` identifier that matches the heading emitted by every page template.

items.title: next: port the classic benchmark suite
items.body:
Closes cutover-prerequisite **row 3.2** (`next/docs/cutover-plan.md` is deliberately left untouched — PR #641 owns that file).

`next/CLAUDE.md` names **benchmarks** in the strict-superset list. Classic declares 8 bench targets (`wingfoil/Cargo.toml:237-268` + the `aeron` group); next declared 3 (`tiers`, `custom_op`, `store_baseline`), none of them twins. This ports all 8 across, plus the harness and features they need.

## What landed

**Harness + features** (`next/crates/wingfoil-next/`)

- `src/bencher.rs`, behind a new `bench` feature with an optional `criterion` dependency — the twin of classic's `bench`-gated `bencher` module, exposing `add_bench`. The trigger node is a `custom_node` declared `Activation::ALWAYS` (classic's `state.always_callback()`), `Tick::Value`/`Tick::Quiet` replace `Ok(true)`/`Ok(false)`, and the end-signal sink replaces `.produce(..)`. Classic's `Signal` conversion tests and the three trigger-cycle tests are ported alongside (6 tests, green).
- `dhat-heap` feature, mirroring classic's, plus `dhat` and `rxrust` dev-dependencies.

**Bench targets** — same names, same `required-features` gating as classic, so `cargo bench --bench <name>` is the same invocation on either tree:

| Target | Features | Engine-touching? |
|---|---|---|
| `graph` | `bench` | ✅ rewired |
| `nanotime` | — | verbatim (shared `NanoTime`) |
| `bfs_vs_dfs_wingfoil` | `bench` | ✅ rewired |
| `bfs_vs_dfs_reactive` | — | verbatim (measures rxrust) |
| `bfs_vs_dfs_async_streams` | `async` | verbatim (measures tokio) |
| `iceoryx2` | `iceoryx2` | verbatim (shared `Burst<T>`) |
| `iceoryx2_modes` | `iceoryx2` | ✅ rewired |
| `aeron_publication_latency` | `aeron` | import path only |
| `aeron_subscription_throughput` | `aeron` | import path only |
| `aeron_transceiver` | `aeron` | import path only |
| `aeron_allocation_tracking` | `aeron` (+`dhat-heap`) | import path only |

**Docs**

- `benches/README.md` — new, catalogues all 11 targets including the three existing next-only ones, the run commands, what the ports changed and what they did not, and restates that benches are not a CI gate.
- `benches/bfs_vs_dfs/README.md` — port of classic's, with `diagram.png` / `diagram.py` / `plot.py` carried over.
- `next/docs/port-plan.md` — surgical: the Phase 6 "Benchmarks" bullet records the port, and the two adapter notes that said the aeron/iceoryx2 benches were "**not** ported" are corrected. Nothing else touched.

## Workload changes

The rule was: keep the workload, change only what the engine forces. Every deviation is documented in the relevant bench's own module doc.

- `graph` — `merge(vec)` → `merge_all` (one `MergeN` node either way, so `width*depth + 2` nodes, matching classic exactly); `map(std::hint::black_box)` → `map(|i: &u64| std::hint::black_box(*i))` because next's `map` takes `&T`; the builder closure is `(&GraphBuilder, &Stream<()>) -> Upstream` rather than `Rc<dyn Node> -> Rc<dyn Node>`.
- `bfs_vs_dfs_wingfoil` — classic's free `add(&s, &s)` (a `bimap` with *both* upstreams active) is `s.join(&s, |a, b| a + b)`, next's two-active-input combine. One node per level either way, so the 2^N-paths shape the bench exists to measure is unchanged.
- `iceoryx2_modes` — wired through `GraphBuilder` + `Runner::run` instead of `Graph::new(vec[..]).run()`; `iceoryx2_sub_opts` takes the run mode and returns `Result` (next rejects a historical subscription at wiring) so the call is `?`-propagated; the publisher is the `Iceoryx2SinkOps::iceoryx2_pub_with` extension method; `ticker(..).produce(closure)` → `ticker(..).map(closure)`; `collapse().collect()` → `collapse().accumulate()`. Node count and shape unchanged, graph construction still inside the timed body as classic has it.
- `nanotime` and `iceoryx2` measure types next *re-exports* from classic (`NanoTime`, `Burst<T>`), so both trees compile identical code. The targets exist for suite completeness and to keep the invocations working after the cutover; the module docs say so explicitly, so nobody reads a "difference" into two bars of the same function.
- The `bfs_vs_dfs_reactive` / `_async_streams` baselines and the four `aeron_*` benches drive other libraries or ported backends with identical signatures — verbatim apart from the crate in the import path.
- `plot.py` carries classic's measured arrays with a header noting they are a *reading*, to be refilled from a next run. `latency.png` and `benches/images/` (criterion report output on one specific CPU) are deliberately **not** duplicated — they are results, not source, and shipping classic's numbers under a next heading would be misleading. Both READMEs link to the classic captures and say how to regenerate.

## Not done, on purpose

Benches are **not** wired as a CI gate. `next/docs/port-plan.md` defers that deliberately (criterion wall-clock thresholds are too noisy on shared runners); the suite stays a run-on-demand scaffold and the READMEs point at the deterministic perf gates, which are tests.

`wingfoil/benches/` is untouched — classic keeps shipping until Phase 7 and is the parity oracle.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` ✅
- `cargo lint` ✅ (`--workspace --all-targets`, default features)
- `cargo lint-all` ✅ (`--all-features`, so every bench target above compiles under `-D warnings`, including the `aeron` and `iceoryx2` ones)
- `cargo test -p wingfoil-next --features bench --lib bencher` ✅ 6/6

**Sandbox note:** the `aeron` targets needed CMake ≥ 3.30 (`rusteron-client`'s bundled Aeron C build), and this sandbox shipped 3.28.3. I installed CMake 3.31 per the repo-root `CLAUDE.md` instructions and then compiled all four `aeron_*` benches successfully — so nothing was dropped or left unverified. Benches were *compiled*, not *run*: the aeron and iceoryx2 targets need a live media driver / shared memory, and criterion numbers from a shared sandbox would not be meaningful anyway.

items.title: feat(bench): Spanish-correct WER normalization protocol
items.body:
Implements `.scratch/perf-roadmap/issues/06-spanish-wer-normalization-protocol.md`.

## Why

The **Quality Benchmark** built its normalized metric lane by stripping ASCII
punctuation with `str.translate` and collapsing whitespace. That protocol was
invented locally rather than adopted, so the numbers it produced were not
comparable to any published Spanish WER, and the project had no way to tell
whether a change improved quality or merely moved the yardstick.

## What changed

**Protocol.** Normalized scoring now uses the **Basic Text Normalizer** OpenAI
used to report Whisper WER for every non-English language: bracketed and
parenthesised content removed, lowercased, symbols and punctuation mapped to
spaces, whitespace collapsed, and **diacritics preserved**. It is applied
identically to the **Reference STM** and the **Hypothesis STM**, on scratch
copies at scoring time, so both artifacts stay intact on disk and the raw lane
remains recoverable.

**Diacritics.** `remove_diacritics` is left at its `False` default and never
exposed as a setting. Enabling it collapses `esta`/`está` and `ano`/`año`,
silently understating Spanish error in the direction that flatters the pipeline.
`EnglishTextNormalizer` is not vendored at all, so it cannot be reached for any
language; a test asserts this and further tests assert Spanish diacritics
survive normalization (including NFC/NFD equivalence).

**Vendored, not depended on.** `coro/bench/normalizers/basic.py` carries ~60
lines of MIT code with its provenance and licence attribution in the docstring.
The upstream package that ships it pulls in Torch and a tokenizer stack the
benchmark does not need, and vendoring pins the protocol so an upstream change
cannot silently move reported numbers. `split_letters` is retained from upstream
with its `regex` import deferred into the branch that uses it, so no import-time
dependency is added.

**Two lanes, always labelled.** Both the **Raw Metric Lane** and the
**Normalized Metric Lane** are reported per **Workload Item** and in the
run-level aggregate. The rendered report (GFM markdown and rich stdout) names
the lane in each table heading and states its protocol in a caption, so no
figure is readable without knowing what produced it. DER is called out as
lane-independent — it scores speaker time, not text — and reported once.

**Robustness.** A normalized lane whose normalization leaves either side with no
scoreable lines (e.g. a segment that was only a `[non-speech]` marker) is
skipped with a warning on stderr rather than raising, so it cannot take the raw
lane and DER down with it.

**Docs.** ADR 0008 records the decision and rejected alternatives. `CONTEXT.md`
gains **Basic Text Normalizer**, **Metric Lane**, **Raw Metric Lane** and
**Normalized Metric Lane**, plus relationships, dialogue, and the resolved
ambiguity.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Normalized scoring uses the diacritic-preserving basic normalizer, applied
      identically to **Reference STM** and **Hypothesis STM**.
- [x] The English-specific normalizer is not used for any language, and a test
      asserts Spanish diacritics survive normalization.
- [x] Both raw and normalized lanes appear per **Workload Item** and in the
      run-level aggregate, and the rendered report labels which lane each figure
      came from.
- [x] An ADR records the protocol decision and its rationale.
- [x] `CONTEXT.md` gains the vocabulary for the two lanes.
- [x] `uvx prek run --all-files` and `uv run pytest` pass.

## Verification

- `uvx prek run --all-files` — all hooks pass.
- `uv run pytest` — 508 passed, 5 skipped (env synced as CI does:
  `uv sync --frozen --extra cpu --group bench`; `meeteval` lives in the `bench`
  group, which is not a default group).
- Both run under `systemd-run` with `MemoryMax`/`CPUQuota`; wall/peak-RSS stats
  in `.tmp/logs/`. Peak RSS for the full suite: ~1.3 GB, wall ~3m37s.

No benchmark run is claimed here: this issue changes how figures are computed,
it does not assert a quality improvement.

## Notes for reviewers

**This changes reported numbers.** Any benchmark figure recorded before this
branch is not comparable to figures recorded after it. Comparisons across that
boundary must be re-run, not reused.

**Behaviour change worth knowing:** under the old protocol a segment reading
`[laughs]` normalized to `laughs` and was scored as a word. Under the Whisper
protocol it normalizes to nothing and the line is dropped from both sides. That
is the intended protocol behaviour, not a regression.

**Out of scope, noted not fixed:**

- `README.md` (~line 429) reports an "ORC-WER (norm)" leaderboard produced under
  the old protocol, and its caption does not name the protocol. Those figures
  are now stale by the rule above. `README.md` is issue 01's primary file per
  the PRD's file-ownership table, so it is left untouched here; it needs a
  re-run plus a caption naming the **Normalized Metric Lane**.
- `docs/adr/` has two files numbered `0002` (`0002-meeteval-for-quality-scoring`
  and `0002-replace-chunked-file-with-streaming-pipeline`) and no `0004`. This
  PR adds `0008`, following the highest existing number; the collision predates
  it and is not renumbered here.
- The quality summary JSON still spells the raw lane as bare `cpwer`/`orcwer`/
  `dicpwer` keys rather than an explicit `raw` block. Renaming would break
  existing artifacts and downstream readers; the lane labelling required by this
  issue is delivered in the rendered report, and the model docstrings now name
  which lane each field belongs to.

`coro/settings.py` is untouched.

items.title: perf: O(1) select-by-ID in DBSQLMemoryAdapter; add JSON and DB benchmarks
items.body:
Adds JSON and DB benchmark suites, and one optimization they turned up.

## The optimization: O(1) select-by-ID in `DBSQLMemoryAdapter`

`_selectEntries` answered *every* condition by scanning the table `Map` and evaluating the condition per row — including a `ConditionID`, even though that `Map` is keyed by ID and the adapter already has an O(1) lookup helper. So `selectByID` was O(rows):

| rows | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 7.80 µs | 7.13 µs |
| 50 | 9.73 µs | 7.16 µs |
| 400 | 25.26 µs | **7.22 µs** |

Now flat. A lookup miss falls through to the original scan, so a `ConditionID` whose value doesn't match a key exactly (a `String` `'7'` against an `int` `7`) resolves exactly as before — just as slowly as it always did. Results are unchanged either way.

This mostly speeds up the test suite and development, since the memory adapter is where those run.

## A correction

An earlier commit on this branch claimed the cost of a query "is the repository/transaction machinery". **That was wrong**, and I'd published it before checking. Scaling the row count shows `selectByQuery` is linear:

| rows | `selectByQuery` |
|---|---|
| 10 | 10.9 µs |
| 50 | 20.4 µs |
| 400 | 105.9 µs |

≈ 8.5 µs fixed + ~0.24 µs/row. The number was dominated by the memory adapter's scan, which a real SQL adapter never pays. Only the fixed part is shared framework cost. `benchmark/README.md`, the CHANGELOG and the in-file comments now say so, and the DB suite takes `--rows=N` so the two can be separated.

## What the suites show otherwise

**JSON needs nothing.** `Json.encodeToSink` — the response path — runs close to a bare `dart:convert` encode (~1.5 µs vs ~1.2 µs, small map) and is *faster* on larger payloads, since it writes bytes to a sink instead of building a `String`. Request bodies go through `dart:convert` directly, so there's no layer to remove.

**DB**, at 50 rows:

| | µs/op |
|---|---|
| `ConditionParseCache.parseQuery` (cached) | 0.010 |
| `Entity.toJson` | 0.074 |
| `generateSelectSQL` | 0.83 |
| `EntityHandler.createFromMap` | 1.12 |
| `ConditionParser.parse` (shared parser) | 2.74 |
| `Transaction.executeBlock` (**empty**) | 2.43 |
| `repository.selectByID` | 7.26 |

The two things a query is assumed to be expensive for are not: parsing is cached at ~300× cheaper than parsing, and SQL generation is under a microsecond.

## Two hypotheses that failed

Recorded so they aren't re-tried:

1. **Per-response `JsonEncoder`.** `Json._buildJsonEncoder` returns the cached `defaultEncoder` only when *every* argument is defaulted — and the response path always passes `toEncodable`, so it builds a fresh encoder each time. Memoizing it (safe: `autoResetEntityCache` defaults to `true`) moved the small-map encode **1.555 → 1.522 µs** and made the 50-map case slightly *worse*. Noise.
2. **Eager `Completer`s.** `Transaction` creates three in its constructor despite the fields being `late final`. Making them lazy left an empty `executeBlock` at **2.40 µs**, unchanged.

Neither is included.

## Another measurement error worth flagging

My first DB run reported `ConditionParser.parse` at **125 µs**, which looked like a major find. It was my benchmark constructing a `ConditionParser` per iteration — the cost is PetitParser building the grammar lazily. `bones_api` holds it in a `static final`, so it's a one-off startup cost and there's no bug. The corrected benchmark reuses the parser (2.74 µs), with a note in the README since a per-query parser *would* be catastrophic.

## Where to look next

`Transaction.executeBlock` — 2.4 µs for an *empty* block is the floor under every DB operation and the largest remaining fixed cost. That wants a real profiler (`dart run --observe`), not more micro-benchmarks.

The DB suite carries a small self-contained `BenchUser` entity so it doesn't depend on the test fixtures.

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `dart test --exclude-tags docker` | 783 passed |
| `dart analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings .` | clean |
