items.title: Integrate ExtractBench extraction benchmark
items.body:
## What

This PR integrates the complete ExtractBench system into this repository, reframing it from a parse-only benchmark into a benchmark for **schema-guided extraction** from enterprise documents. Given a document and a user-defined JSON Schema, a system must return schema-valid JSON with the correct values, every record of each repeated structure, missing fields marked `null` rather than invented, and source evidence for each value. All existing parse capabilities are preserved.

The benchmark covers **370 documents (4,869 pages)** across 8 business domains and 67 document types, each type with its own schema, tagged along five independent difficulty axes (task challenge, perception challenge, table structure, length, business domain).

## Why

Enterprises write a new schema for almost every workflow, so an extraction system cannot be tuned to a fixed template — it has to handle schemas and documents it has never seen. Because agents increasingly act on extracted values before anyone reviews them, one truncated schedule or one invented value becomes a wrong payment or a wrong decision. The benchmark therefore scores completeness and traceability: unified value F1 as the headline metric, plus word- and page-level grounding F1.

## How

The integration lands as a single squashed change so the repository moves atomically from the parse-only baseline to the full extraction benchmark. Recent parse-side changes on `main` that postdate the extraction work (oi_parser, MinerU-Diffusion, Nemotron-Omni, Gemini 3.6 Flash / 3.5 Flash Lite pipelines, Extend Light, `bbox_scale` coordinate-frame config, formatting-rule fixes) were reconciled and transposed into the renamed package so nothing on `main` is lost.

## Changes

- **Package rename**: `parse_bench` -> `extract_bench` across source, tests, tooling, and project metadata; project renamed to `extract-bench`.
- **Extract task type, end to end**: extraction schemas and test-case loading, inference routing, evaluation metrics (value F1 with per-split precision/recall, row-identity scoring for repeated structures, word- and page-level grounding), and cost accounting.
- **Extract providers and pipelines**: LlamaExtract (Agentic, Agentic Plus, Cost-Effective), coding agents (Claude Code, Codex), direct model APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI Responses, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, vLLM open-weight, NuExtract3), and specialized APIs (Reducto, Extend, Datalab, Pulse, Landing AI, Azure Content Understanding, Lift, table-codegen), with citation and grounding support.
- **Analysis and reporting suite**: leaderboard, aggregation, comparison, and detailed per-document HTML reports with grounding bbox visualization, unified metric selectors, failed-document reporting, and static CSS/JS assets.
- **Leaderboard**: `leaderboard.csv` and README tables now report extract metrics (unified value F1 by length split, word/page grounding F1, cost per page).
- **Runtime hardening**: lazy adapter registry, lazily initialized sub-CLIs, dependency shaving, graceful test skips when runner extras are absent, and a CI workflow (ruff + pytest with and without runner extras).
- **Preserved upstream parse work**, transposed into the new layout: oi_parser provider/pipeline/label mapper/layout adapter; MinerU-Diffusion and Nemotron-Omni pipelines; Gemini 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash Lite pipelines; Extend Light pipeline with `extend-ai>=1.16.0`; `bbox_scale` config gated to providers that pin the perceived image frame; `items_to_markdown` delimiter fix and single-span formatting-rule matching, with their regression tests.
- **Housekeeping**: annotator apps and local data directories are no longer tracked.

## Testing

- Full suite with runner extras: **774 passed**.
- Runner-free suite (matches CI's first stage): **687 passed, 20 skipped**, with the graceful-skip convention applied to the transposed coordinate-frame tests.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean; `uv lock` verified consistent with `pyproject.toml` (`uv sync --locked`).
- Verified file-by-file that the diff against the extraction codebase is limited to the transposed upstream parse commits listed above.

## Notes

- The PR is intentionally a single commit; review is best done by area (schemas, metrics, providers, analysis) rather than commit-by-commit.
- Breaking change for downstream consumers: the Python package import path changes from `parse_bench` to `extract_bench`, and `leaderboard.csv` switches to the extract-metric schema.
- New optional environment variables are documented in `.env.example`; no defaults changed for existing parse pipelines beyond the documented `bbox_scale` gating.

items.title: Correct the guidance the measured workspace carries
items.body:
## What Changed

A full read of `benchmark/instructions/**` (21 files) and every `AGENTS.md` and skill under `benchmark/template/**` (26 files), checked against the template source, found five problems. All five are fixed here.

## The workspace told the cell it was being benchmarked

`EvidenceBenchmarkSupervision.ts:459` refuses an operator warning whose text matches `benchmark`, `operator`, `auditor`, `verdict`, `supervisor`, `reviewer`, `plugin`, `(another|other|external|main|measurement) agent`, or `(plain|evidence) (arm|mode|agent)`. The stated reason is that a cell told it is being measured stops being a measurement.

The template said it anyway, in documents the cell is instructed to read in full:

| Where | What it said |
| --- | --- |
| `project/SKILL.md:42` | "**The benchmark arms** intentionally use different watcher lifecycles; never carry one arm's lifecycle into another." |
| `backend/SKILL.md:79` | "**The benchmark arms** intentionally use different lifecycles; never infer one arm's lifecycle from another." |
| `project/SKILL.md:80`, `backend/SKILL.md:108` | "**the current arm's** instruction" |
| `evidence/SKILL.md:170` | "**Only this arm** uses:" |
| `evidence/SKILL.md:176` | "the **benchmark** graph workload is frozen" |
| `project/SKILL.md:3`, `frontend/design.md:3`, `package.json:5`, `README.md:3,21` | "benchmark" as a descriptor |
| `vite.config.ts:17`, `.gitignore:3` | `.benchmark-cache/` |

The first two are the worst: they disclose not just the measurement but the existence of a second arm that differs deliberately. Everything now speaks of the current objective, and the cache directory is `.build-cache`.

The `<!-- benchmark-template-splice: base-body -->` marker stays, because `EvidenceBenchmarkWorkspace.applyOverlay` consumes it during preparation and it never reaches a workspace.

## Plain's Backend Final gated on a process its arm had not started

`plain/backend/final.md` required backend `pnpm dev` to be running "through Overall Final". That server exists to serve the frontend during live integration — `project/SKILL.md:44` and `backend/SKILL.md:99` both place it there — and Plain first requires it at `plain/frontend/start.md:7`, one stage later.

A cell following its instructions literally could not check its own box at Backend Final. The stage keeps `check:watch` and `pnpm test`, which are the backend gates.

## Evidence's instructions and skill disagreed about runtime tests

`evidence/SKILL.md:191` told the cell to "run the phase's runtime tests" at each gate. No Evidence instruction checklist asked for one after Backend Start and Frontend Start, and the checklist is what keeps a Goal active, so the skill sentence bound nothing.

The reruns are now explicitly the cell's judgement. A cell reaches Review having already passed compile and runtime at Start, and a Review correction is usually a tag rather than a behavior, so each Final states the tradeoff — the watcher reports type and lint diagnostics only — and leaves the decision to the agent. No checklist item was added, because a checklist item is a completion gate rather than a discretion.

## Plain's dry-loop machinery lived in the shared base

`base/backend/testing.md` carried the mutation calibration paragraph, phrased around "a backend or overall review that may qualify as clean". That is Plain's dry-loop vocabulary for a procedure the Evidence arm does not run, sitting in a document both arms read in full.

It moves to `plain/review/SKILL.md`, beside the rules that already explain why a calibration invalidates the round it ran in. The base keeps the arm-neutral rule that tests should fail against random-answer stubs.

## Test sufficiency was dictated by count

Operation Ownership demanded "at least two tests per operation", "one success case", and "at least one non-success case", and `plain/review/backend.md` made a single-test accessor a finding on the ground that one test cannot prove both a working path and a refusal.

That decides for the agent how much proof a requirement deserves, including for operations whose requirements state no refusal at all. The floor is now one test per published operation. How much further to go is judged from the requirements, and the review asks whether a behavior the requirements state is unproven rather than counting tests.

`testing.md` keeps one related rule: do not prove an operation's success and refusal inside a single test. It constrains structure only when the agent has already chosen to test both, and never forces a refusal test to exist.

## Verified

Every claim above was read against the template source before the edit:

- `packages/backend` really defines a `dev` script (`ttsx src/executable/server.ts`), so the Plain gate was misplaced rather than impossible.
- `VITE_API_SIMULATE` really exists (`packages/frontend/src/lib/config.ts:11`).
- The `Configured Claims` table matches the four `lint.config.ts` files exactly — all eight claims, in the configurations named.
- `packages/api/package.json` exports only `.`, as `api/SKILL.md` and `project/SKILL.md` require.
- `packages/backend/tsconfig.json` really maps `@prisma/sdk`, and `test/tsconfig.json` really includes `.` and `../src`.
- Only `.benchmark-cache` referenced the renamed path, in `.gitignore` and `vite.config.ts`.

Sweeps: no `benchmark`, `current arm`, or `the arms` remains in `benchmark/template/**` or `benchmark/instructions/**`; no mojibake, BOM, or CRLF in any changed file; `base/package.json` still parses.

Not verified: nothing executable in this repository changed, so no build, lint, or test was run. `pnpm format` does not apply — `benchmark/template` is not a workspace member and nothing in this repository compiles or formats it.

## Left Alone Deliberately

The scaffold `HealthController` carries no `@evidence` tag while the Evidence overlay ships a pre-tagged health test. The owner considers the health endpoint an example the cell may handle as it sees fit, so it stays as is.

`rg` remains the accessor-index and `@todo` scan tool in all five call sites. It is the most precise instrument for the job, and a replacement built on `git grep -E '@accessor \S+'` would depend on a GNU extension that portable ERE does not guarantee.

items.title: docs: correct the five surviving docs-vs-code divergences (#1305)
items.body:
Closes #1305. Parent: #1163.

Docs only — no product code, no defaults, no test changes.

## Where this came from

#1163 listed 13 docs-vs-code divergences with 0 of its 26 acceptance criteria ever ticked, which reads as 13 open items. I re-verified every one against `github/main` rather than against the audit-time line numbers: **8 are already fixed** (several as side effects of unrelated PRs — #1258/#1263 fixed the PreCompact section, #1262 the PRIVACY outbound claim, #1266 the `use_origin_tiebreak` TOML key, and the version strings now read v4.2.0). The audit is posted on the umbrella. **These are the 5 that survive.**

## The corrections

**1. The non-blocking contract was false in both halves.** `ARCHITECTURE.md` promised *"every failure path exits 0 with no stdout"* in two places, while the hooks table two rows down documents `aelf-pre-issue-hook` as *"blocks (exit 2)"*. Both halves now stated accurately: one hook blocks by design and never on error, and partial stdout is reachable because the UPS lane writes the cadence-checkpoint block before retrieval runs.

**2. The enrichment boundary recorded none of what it claimed.** The bullet said model id, version and prompt-template hash are recorded. `scanner.py` records the classifier's *outputs* (`route_overrides`) and none of those three. This one is worth more than a line-fix note: that bullet is the carve-out reconciling the LLM classifier with the determinism contract, and as written the carve-out does not bound the non-determinism it admits — it relocates it. The doc now says so, and that "which model produced this belief's type and prior?" is unanswerable from the store. **Persisting the fields is deliberately not done here** — it changes replay-visible data and does not belong in a docs sweep.

**3. The headline benchmark claim was unfalsifiable.** `README.md`'s +0.2851 / +94.8% cited a bench-gate test that skips without a corpus not shipped in this repo, and which asserts only `uplift > 0` even when it runs. Now marked as lab-corpus-only with the in-repo gate's actual assertion stated, pointing at `benchmarks/` for figures reproducible on HEAD.

**4. The badge contradicted the architecture doc.** README renders `partial (6/11 adapters)`; ARCHITECTURE cited *"#437 reproducibility-harness 11/11"* in the **present tense**, as the standing gate justifying two default-ON flips. 11/11 was true at the v2.1.0 cut; the badge reflects a later regression. Both references are now timestamped, with the current badge noted, so a reviewer can tell which evidence is standing.

**5. The layering invariant was false.** *"Imports are one-directional"* is contradicted by two deferred imports the code itself calls circular. Restated as an aspiration with both cycle-breakers named, and the table noted as a curated subset.

## Verification

Every corrected string was re-grepped against `main` — the failure mode being fixed is text that was true when written, so the fix has to be checked the same way:

| claim written | verified against |
|---|---|
| the guard exits 2 | `pre_issue_create_hook.py:434` |
| cadence block precedes retrieval | `hook.py:959` |
| `raw_meta` carries `route_overrides` only | `scanner.py:268-286` |
| two deferred cycle-breakers | `store.py:3816`, `classification.py:230` |
| 31 table rows, 117 modules | counted on `main` |

The audit's own figure of "~113 `.py` files" was **wrong** — it is 117 today; I counted rather than copying it.

Discretion grep on added lines: clean. Two atomic commits, one per file.

## Summary by Sourcery

Clarify and correct documentation around determinism, enrichment, module layering, hooks non-blocking behavior, benchmarking claims, and reproducibility status to align with current code and benchmarks.

Documentation:
- Update enrichment-layer determinism description to reflect that only sentence/source and classifier outputs are stored, not model identity or prompt template metadata.
- Restate module import layering as an aspirational, partially violated invariant and note that the table is a curated subset of modules, not an exhaustive map.
- Clarify the hooks non-blocking contract, explicitly documenting the deliberate blocking behavior of the pre-issue hook and the possibility of partial stdout.
- Qualify the composition tracker and reproducibility-harness claims with timestamps and current badge status to distinguish past gate evidence from present harness state.
- Revise README benchmark documentation to mark headline uplift figures as lab-corpus-only and point to in-repo, reproducible benchmarks instead.

items.title: fix(setup): make the benchmark runnable from a cold start
items.body:
Reviewed the setup guide from the position of a new user: kubectl only, new Kubernetes cluster, own Docker Hub repo, no images, no namespace, no CI, new laptop. Five things would have stopped that user. None were visible from inside our cluster, where every default already happened to be correct.

## Portability fixes

**The scripts required `oc`; the READMEs documented `kubectl`.** 54 call sites across 8 executables. All 12 subcommands in use (`apply create delete exec get logs patch port-forward rollout scale set wait`) are standard kubectl, so every call site is converted. OpenShift users are unaffected, kubectl works there too.

**`deploy/prometheus.yaml` was never applied by anything.** `values-baseline-kvaware.yaml` deliberately disables the subchart's Prometheus and defers to this manifest, but no script applied it and no README mentioned it. A new user would run a full 2.5-hour sweep and only then discover the load imbalance co-primary, the headline result, had no data. Now an explicit step 1 command with a line saying why it is required.

**Two layers of hardcoded cluster URLs.** `BASE_URL` defaulted to our OpenShift route in three scripts. Separately, `registry-probe.sh` carried its own hardcoded default under a *different* variable name (`URL`, not `BASE_URL`), and `run_cell.sh` invoked it passing no environment at all, so a user who set `BASE_URL` correctly still had the probe gating on our cluster. Defaults now match the documented port-forward, the probe derives its URL from `BASE_URL`, and both callers pass `NS`/`BASE_URL`/`MODEL` explicitly.

**`ROUTER_REPO`** replaces a repo name that was hardcoded in `run_cell.sh` and set independently in the values file, so the deployed image and the asserted image could silently disagree. It is now both `--set` to helm and asserted against the running pod from one variable.

**`storageClass` is ODF-specific and RWX.** Engine pods hang in Pending on any other cluster with no obvious cause. Now documented as a required change with `kubectl get storageclass` to find yours.

## Documentation

- **Prerequisites section** added: laptop tools with versions, cluster requirements (2 GPUs on 2 nodes, 23GB each, GPU Operator, RWX storage class, exact permissions needed), and the values that must change per cluster.
- **Step 2 rewritten** for a manual build: `docker.io/<username>` naming, repo root as build context, `podman login`/`push`, and the note that both repos must be public because nothing creates an image pull secret.
- **File-call map** for the sweep, so you can see what calls what.
- **Why the TTFT result is a null**, new section. `fig5-percentiles` shows lower bars for `loadaware` and the report says the result is not significant; that reads as a contradiction until you know the seed spread overlaps and the CI contains zero. Also explains that `beta=1.0` looking better is a post-hoc selection across five betas, not a claim.
- **All 12 figures** described, with the 4 the report uses marked.
- **Step 6 split** into explained snippets. The goodput section is gone, its command folded in as one more `--metric`.
- **Known cluster problems section removed**; each fix is now a comment at the code that applies it.
- **Seeds rationale rewritten** to explain what a seed is and why 20, without the Wilcoxon internals.
- **18 stale code comments** fixed that pointed at README sections which no longer existed after the earlier rewrite.
- `.venv/` added to `.gitignore`, since both READMEs tell the reader to create it.

## Verification

- 194 tests pass
- `./scripts/reproduce.sh` regenerates every reported number from committed data
- Every README section reference in code resolves to a real heading (checked mechanically)
- `bash -n` / AST / YAML parse on all 26 changed files

No measurement data changed. The reported numbers are untouched.

items.title: Codex/phase15 correctness 2026 07 28
items.body:
## Summary

This PR completes the implementation portion of Phase 15: testing, chaos validation, benchmarking and diagnostics.

It adds the remaining `relish test`, `relish bench`, `relish wtf` and `relish trace` foundations, along with the capability evidence, resource ownership and safety controls required to make their results trustworthy.

The guiding rule is simple: unsupported, unobserved or inconclusive behaviour must never become a green result.

## What changed

### Conclusive test results

- Defines explicit `Pass`, `Fail`, `Skipped` and `Unknown` outcomes.
- Treats timeouts, panics, incomplete evidence and unverified cleanup as inconclusive.
- Adds full acceptance profiles where required skips and unknown evidence fail.
- Introduces inherited absolute deadlines so setup, execution and cleanup share one bounded lifetime.
- Preserves cleanup failures independently from the test result.

### Live capability and readiness evidence

- Publishes authenticated, expiring capability evidence for each node.
- Distinguishes available, unavailable and unknown capabilities.
- Adds live readiness state for critical Bun subsystems.
- Includes runtime, kernel, build and topology fingerprints.
- Bounds cross-node collection and retains explicit evidence for unreachable nodes.

### Durable test resource ownership

- Adds durable, bounded application and namespace leases.
- Persists leases in standalone mode and replicates them through Raft in clustered mode.
- Reaps abandoned resources after runner death, restart or leader failover.
- Makes cleanup exact and ownership-based rather than namespace-wide.
- Pins the Phase 15 container workload to an immutable multi-architecture BusyBox OCI index.
- Keeps ProcessGrill as a separate portable profile.
- Fixes command execution inside Apple Container workloads.

### Chaos primitives and catalogue

- Adds reversible cluster transport quiescing.
- Implements authenticated node drain and node failure operations.
- Adds bounded, node-scoped CPU and memory pressure on rootful Linux.
- Requires server-owned operation grants, suitable roles and explicit acknowledgement.
- Re-authorises distributed operations on the target node.
- Emits structured audit events bound to the authenticated principal.
- Makes network fault support honest: delay and bandwidth faults refuse execution because the current cgroup hooks cannot implement packet pacing.
- Adds five guarded serial scenarios:

  1. Leader failure and re-election
  2. Dead-worker rescheduling
  3. Minority partition
  4. Bounded node pressure
  5. Node failure during deployment

- Missing node-failure or pressure prerequisites cause refusal, not a green skip.
- Fault cleanup uses exact IDs and runs after success, failure, timeout or panic.

### Real data-plane benchmarks

- Adds a versioned benchmark report and comparison contract.
- Records topology, runtime, kernel and build fingerprints.
- Refuses incompatible comparisons.
- Reports missing metrics explicitly.
- Marks noisy hosted results as informational.
- Exercises service discovery through a DNS query from the source workload.
- Exercises network throughput through `.internal` DNS and the service VIP.
- Requires explicit acknowledgement for disruptive and capacity benchmarks.
- Uses server-owned leases and cleanup for every suite.

### `relish wtf`

- Adds a deterministic diagnosis engine with schema-v1 output.
- Separates critical, warning, unknown and healthy findings.
- Correlates deploy activity, restart windows, logs, resolver state and live instances.
- Adds bounded authenticated telemetry for:

  - Council and node health
  - Deploy activity
  - Crash loops
  - Disk capacity
  - CPU throttling
  - Certificate lifecycle
  - Registry redundancy
  - Alerts and active faults

- Supports application scoping and watch mode.
- Uses the command exit contract:

  - `0`: healthy
  - `1`: diagnosed failure
  - `2`: incomplete or unknown evidence

### `relish trace`

- Runs the DNS and TCP probes from the selected source workload.
- Uses fixed positional command arguments rather than arbitrary shell execution.
- Reads live userspace service state.
- Reads attached Linux eBPF backend and firewall maps where available.
- Labels evidence as observed, inferred or unavailable.
- Returns `Unknown` when the evidence cannot support a conclusion.
- Bounds per-node concurrency and refuses excess requests rather than queueing them.
- Restricts external probes behind:

  - Admin authorisation
  - The `probe_external_destination` operation grant
  - Protected-cluster policy
  - An exact server-owned `host:port` allowlist

### Prerequisite correctness fixes

This work also closes several prerequisites uncovered while implementing Phase 15:

- Makes clustered Pickle listeners peer-reachable and authenticated.
- Carries the configured workload trust domain through application, job, JWT and build identities.
- Preserves rootless networking across Bun replacement.
- Publishes real deployment operation state and bounded history.
- Defines the supported v1 ingress TLS contract.
- Makes repository examples and portable CI checks executable.
- Adds live subsystem readiness and supervised failure evidence.

### Dependency audit follow-up

`cargo audit` reports `RUSTSEC-2026-0235` for `rkyv` 0.7 through:

```text
openraft -> byte-unit -> rust_decimal -> rkyv
```

This is a lock-only optional dependency. `byte-unit` disables `rust_decimal`’s default features, `cargo tree --target all -i rkyv` finds no active path, and Reliaburger neither compiles `rkyv` nor reads rkyv archives.

`rust_decimal` 1.x deliberately pins its optional rkyv integration to 0.7, so substituting rkyv 0.8.17 is not compatible. The PR records a narrow temporary exception which expires on 18 August 2026. It is tracked risk, not claimed as fixed.

## Documentation

Updates include:

- The Phase 15 implementation plan and acceptance runbook
- `docs/progress.md`
- Both READMEs
- Chapter 15
- Test harness, chaos, CLI, Bun, ingress, registry and security designs
- Relevant whitepaper, roadmap and manual sections
- Corrections to earlier claims exposed by executable tests

## Validation

Completed during the implementation:

- `make ci`
  - 3,076 default-feature tests
  - 3,052 no-default-feature tests
  - 41 explicitly classified skips in each run
- `make test-cluster`
  - 22 real multi-node tests passed
- Focused Phase 15 testkit suite
  - 67 tests passed
- Council-focused suite
  - 226 tests passed
- Default and no-default focused benchmark, diagnostics and trace suites
- All-target, all-feature Clippy with warnings denied
- Locked all-target, all-feature build
- Formatting and diff checks
- Audit configuration validation

## Remaining acceptance work

This PR does not claim that Phase 15 is fully accepted in production-like conditions.

The final runbook still needs to run against three independent real nodes or VMs, covering:

- The complete ordinary catalogue
- All five live chaos scenarios
- Quick, disruptive and capacity benchmarks
- Seeded `wtf` diagnoses
- Full source-workload trace paths
- Rootful runc and Apple Container profiles where applicable

The available implementation environment could not honestly represent three independent node-pressure domains. That limitation remains visible in `docs/progress.md`; unsupported scenarios have not been converted into green skips.

items.title: chore: retire pre-2.0 benchmark suite
items.body:
## Summary

- removes all five files in the unmaintained `bench/` tree (1,362 lines)
- records the retirement and absence of a maintained 2.0 replacement in the release notes
- labels active README storage figures as historical estimates and removes the unsupported “current benchmark” WAL claim
- corrects the blueprint claim that the 32-partition ceiling is CI performance-validated

## Evidence

The suite was run against the current 2.0 payload on PostgreSQL 17.9 in an isolated cluster/database:

- `run_bench.sql`: exit 0 with 31 errors, then printed `DONE`
- `simulate_1year.sql`: exit 0 with 43 errors, then printed `BENCHMARK COMPLETE`
- `year_insert.sql`: exit 0 with 21 errors, then printed `1-YEAR BENCHMARK COMPLETE`
- `full_bench.sh`: exit 1 after invalid synthetic data violated `sample_data_check`
- `year_insert.sh`: exit 1 after its missing installer and obsolete `ash.query_map` errors were masked; it reported millions of rows while the heap remained 8192 bytes

The stale readers were `ash.top_waits`, `ash.top_queries`, `ash.waits_by_type`, `ash.wait_timeline`, and `ash.samples_by_database`. `ash.timeline_chart` was not referenced. The suite also used the obsolete global `ash.query_map`, hardcoded a three-slot layout, and did not exercise any current 2.0 reader or rollup path.

No direct references to the benchmark entrypoints existed in README, docs, CI, the release process, or Make targets. CI never ran the suite.

## Decision and tradeoff

Retirement is safer than a cosmetic rename: a credible replacement needs valid raw/minute/hour fixtures, exact correctness assertions, all current readers, configurable partition counts, repeated measurements, and controlled runner metadata. Estimated rewrite cost is 5-7 engineering days plus runner/storage time; retirement is 2-4 hours.

The owner should overrule only if a reproducible 2.0 performance baseline is itself a release requirement and the release can absorb that rewrite. Retirement gives up an in-repository performance harness in principle, but the deleted suite supplied neither trustworthy 2.0 coverage nor actionable numbers.

## Validation

- `git diff --check`
- confirmed `bench/` has no paths in the resulting tree
- confirmed no direct benchmark entrypoint references remain
- confirmed unsupported `current benchmark` / `CI-benchmarked` wording is gone
- manual review of the changed Markdown

No SQL or runtime behavior is changed. Perform a fresh rebase onto `origin/main` immediately before merge.

Closes #139

items.title: Benchmark concordance on a biomarker-driven answer key, and drop the broken README screenshots
items.body:
Two things in here. The README one is cosmetic, the benchmark one is not.

## The broken screenshots

All six files under docs/screenshots were byte-identical, 6726 bytes each, and every one was a capture of an Internal Server Error page rather than the app. The screenshot run they came from had failed against a backend that was not up, so the repo landing page was showing six copies of an error screen.

Removed the section, deleted the dead PNGs, and pulled the same block out of scripts/_write_readme.py, which regenerates the README and would have put it right back on the next run. Also removed the demo GIF line just above it since it pointed into the same now-empty folder. Worth regenerating these properly with the stack actually running at some point, but six error screenshots is worse than none.

## Why the 15.1% is not an accuracy problem

The concordance pilot's 15.1% exact Top-3 keeps getting read as the ranking algorithm being inaccurate. I do not think that is what it measures.

Measured straight off that pilot's own answer key, without reference to anything the pipeline produced:

| observation | value |
|---|---|
| sunitinib in TCGA-KIRC | 20 patients across **16 different** sequenced genes |
| bevacizumab in TCGA-KIRC | 13 patients, 8 genes |
| sorafenib in TCGA-KIRC | 12 patients, 9 genes |
| TCGA-PRAD | top 5 drugs cover **10/10** patients |

Those patients did not share a gene, they shared a diagnosis. That is era standard-of-care prescribing. Reproducing it would mean emitting sunitinib for 16 unrelated genes, which the engine can only do by ignoring the gene, which is the one thing it must not do. That diagnostic ships as scripts/diagnose_concordance_dataset.py so it is reproducible, and it never consults our own output.

## The new benchmark

Added an answer key where the biomarker provably did drive the drug: the NCI-MATCH subprotocol arms. Each is a published expert-committee decision of the form "patients with biomarker X receive drug Y", which is the same question this engine answers. Fetched live from ClinicalTrials.gov, not typed in from memory.

**12/32 exact Top-3 (37.5%), 22/32 class Top-3 (68.8%)**, against 15.1% on the TCGA protocol-care key.

Read the exact number against a ceiling of 75%, not 100%. 8 of the 32 arms assign investigational agents (taselisib, GSK2636771, AZD4547, adavosertib, ulixertinib, defactinib) that an approved-drug recommender structurally cannot return. Class-level concordance is the more meaningful figure here since it credits recommending an approved drug of the same mechanism, which is the actionable answer for a patient not enrolled in the trial.

## Keeping it out of the circular trap

We already have a circular benchmark and I did not want to add a second one. build_concordance_labels.py has a DRUG_BIOMARKER_MAP that infers each patient's gene from the drug they were given, so asking the pipeline "which drug for that gene" is guaranteed to match. That is where the 100% class-adjusted (36/36) figure in ONCOLOGIST_CONCORDANCE_PLAIN_LANGUAGE.md comes from, and it should not be quoted as accuracy.

Three things keep this one honest:

- arms are parsed mechanically and never included or dropped based on whether we got them right
- where an arm names a specific variant, that exact variant is used
- where an arm names only a generic mutation, the variant is chosen by real-world prevalence in MSK-IMPACT rather than by hand, because hand-picking one already known to resolve is exactly how you fake this

That prevalence rule is not uniformly kind to us, which is the point. It moved ERBB2 from exact to miss while moving four other arms into hits.

## What this does not show

The doc says this too, but: NCI-MATCH arms and our OncoKB-derived evidence table are built from the same body of published literature, so agreement is expected. A good score means the table correctly encodes expert consensus actionability. It is not evidence of independent discovery, and no patient outcome is tested anywhere here, only drug-assignment agreement. n is 32 arms with no confidence intervals.

The three benchmarks now line up as: 15.1% on a protocol-care key, 37.5%/68.8% on the trial-assignment key, 0.900 Hit@3 on the tumour board holdout. Concordance rises with how biomarker-driven the answer key is. Different metrics on different case mixes though, so they should not be averaged or swapped for one another.

items.title: benchmarks that measure something, and a gate that can fire
items.body:
`bench/baseline.json` has been a placeholder since RFC-0063 landed, so `--compare` reported every bench `new` and exited 0, and the bench job carried `continue-on-error: true` on top of that. Two layers of "cannot fail" over a corpus that measured four files. This makes the benchmarks real and the gate able to fire.

## 1. Coverage

`examples/langbench.vyrn` — 10 rows the corpus did not hold:

- **the map** (RFC-0028): build over 1000 string keys, 1000 hits, 1000 misses. Only `keys()` was timed before.
- **the string builder**: `"\{}"` interpolation, `joinWith`, `split`. `membench` holds `+` and the append spine; the template path and `std/strings` had nothing.
- **both dispatch mechanisms**: a protocol reached through a bound against an RFC-0037 `fn` value. They measure 27.68 µs and 27.67 µs over 10000 calls — which is the claim ("no vtable, no function pointer") as a number rather than as prose.
- **`std/json`**: reader and writer over a 200-member object.

Each row `blackBox`es its inputs, and the two dispatch rows accumulate through a rolling hash — a sum of a loop-invariant call has a closed form and read 1 ns until they did.

**Writing this found a native double-free.** A `Map` key taken from a borrowed `Array<String>` element is not copied, so the array and the map free the same buffer:

```vyrn
let mut ks: Array<String> = []
ks.push("x" + 1.toString())
let mut m: Map<String, Int64> = [:]
m[ks[0]] = 0
print(ks[0])
```

The interpreter answers correctly; the native binary dies with no output, exit 127. `.copy()` on the key fixes it. No example keys a map from an array element, so parity was blind. `mapBuild` writes the `.copy()` and names the defect; filed separately.

**Not covered, and not coverable this way:** the interpreter loop, the checker on a large input, `gen fn` evaluation, and an end-to-end compile. A `bench` block is a Vyrn program compiled to machine code — the front end is Rust that ran before the block existed. `lex()` is the one compiler surface Vyrn can name and the checker refuses it outside a `gen fn`. Timing those needs a second harness, which is a different RFC.

## 2. A real baseline, honestly sourced

The placeholder stays, because it must be seeded from CI hardware. What changes is that seeding is now a copy:

- a new `Assemble a seedable baseline` step merges the per-example `--json` reports into one `baseline.json` in exactly the shape `bench/baseline.json` needs — no `placeholder`, no `_readme`, `benches` concatenated in corpus order;
- it ships inside the existing `bench-json` artifact, so seeding is: open the newest green `CI` run on main, download `bench-json`, `cp baseline.json bench/baseline.json`, commit;
- the `_readme` names that procedure and that job.

Bench names must be unique across the corpus for a merged baseline to mean anything — `--compare` matches on the name alone. A test pins it.

## 3. The gate

`continue-on-error: true` is gone. It was protecting against nothing (a placeholder exits 0 by arithmetic) and disarming everything.

**Threshold `2.0`, one value in the workflow `env:` as `BENCH_THRESHOLD`.** The comparator's default is 1.5, picked before anything was measured. The reasoning for 2.0:

- the statistic compared is the **minimum** of ≥ 31 samples. A stolen timeslice raises the mean and the median; it cannot lower the minimum. Ordinary preemption is filtered before the comparison starts.
- what remains is **fleet spread**, not jitter: `ubuntu-latest` is several CPU models under one label, and a scheduler handing out a different one moves every row at once. A margin a fleet change can cross turns main red for a reason no commit caused, and a gate that cries wolf gets switched off.
- the regressions this project has actually had were algorithmic: census P1 at 52x, the fixed-array element read at 8x, the module-state append spine unbounded. 2.0 catches all of them with room.

No new statistics: the harness already medians within a run and compares on the min; a consecutive-runs rule needs state CI does not have. Lower the number when the artifact history shows the real spread.

Still push-to-main only — comparing a PR runner against main's baseline compares two machines.

## 4. Regression cover beyond timing

Two holes, both closed:

- **Tools that vanish take their gate with them.** `wasmtime()` returns `None` and parity prints `NOTE: no wasmtime` and passes on two engines; `find_node()` does the same and the memory census — the only thing in the repo that can see a leak — skips whole. A restored-but-empty cache, a renamed release asset or a typo in an exported path all read as green. `VYRN_REQUIRE_TOOLS=1` (set once at workflow level) turns both into a panic naming the tool and the variable. The guard lives in the shared `wasmtime()` / `find_node()`, so every call site is covered.
- **The census had no canary.** All 21 rows assert `Steady`, which is also what a measurement that stopped measuring reports — a driver calling nothing, exports that vanished, a `byteLength` read that no longer moves. A new `keptForever` export keeps every buffer in module state on purpose and its row asserts `Leaks`, so the detecting arm is exercised by something. It is not a defect and no phase will flip it.

## 5. Proof

- `vyrn bench examples/langbench.vyrn` — all 10 rows report.
- placeholder baseline → every bench `new`, `no regressions`, exit 0. Verified, not assumed.
- real seeded baseline (merged by the CI step's own program) → all `ok`, exit 0.
- the same baseline with mins quartered → all `REGRESSED`, `10 regressed`, exit 1, factors 3.80–4.10 where 4.0 is exact. Min-to-min drift on one machine inside 5%.
- `cargo test --workspace --release --no-fail-fast`: **1574 passed, 0 failed**.
- `cargo test -p vyrn-cli --release --test parity -- --ignored --test-threads=1` with wasmtime + sysroot + builtins: **37 passed, 0 failed** — `langbench` is a three-way parity citizen.
- `vyrn fmt --check` clean.

`cargo fmt --check` reports two pre-existing diffs (`vyrn-cli/src/main.rs:1568`, `tests/limits.rs:165`) in files this branch does not touch. Left alone.

items.title: feat: Bring the benchmark suite to a production-ready state
items.body:
Brings the v2 rework to a production-ready state: completes it, fixes the bugs found along the way, and adds the tests, linting, CI and documentation the project had none of.

> **Base branch note:** this targets `main` because it contains all of `feat/classes` plus the work that finishes it — `feat/classes` on its own is missing 15 of the 17 trials and its source-display feature, so it was never mergeable alone. Merging this supersedes `feat/classes`, which can then be deleted. Happy to retarget to `feat/classes` if you'd rather review the 8 new commits in isolation.

## Why

`main` (v1, dormant since Sept 2022) produced statistically wrong numbers and froze the game for minutes. `feat/classes` (dormant since June 2023) had the right architecture — a coroutine runner and IQR statistics — but the rewrite left 15 trials behind and commented out the report's source display. Neither branch could publish a report worth trusting, and neither shipped a README, licence, tests or CI.

## What changed

### The v1 tree is gone

Deleted rather than patched — its statistics were superseded. This also surfaced a latent bug: the v2 reporter was still reading `style.css`/`script.js` out of the **v1** directory, so it would have broken the moment v1 was removed.

### Correctness

- **`draw_rect` didn't measure what it claimed.** The function labelled "RoundedBox" actually called `surface.DrawRect` with a wrong signature — the published comparison was meaningless. It now calls `draw.RoundedBox`.
- **Per-call average was `mean / runs`**, not `mean / iterations`.
- **`Statistic` rewritten over an explicitly sorted array.** The old index-replacement scheme could double-replace a rank when a run time collided with an index; bounds are now inclusive, so identical run times and single-run trials are no longer rejected as their own outliers.
- **Introspection serialised the wrong variable** (an undefined global instead of the parameter), mangling every captured string, number and Color. It now also snapshots upvalues *before* the runs mutate them, and iterates `1..nups`.
- **Report sources weren't HTML-escaped** — v1 emitted raw `<` from code like `if b < 0`.
- **`coroutine.isyieldable` doesn't exist in Garry's Mod.** It's Lua 5.2; the public branch ships LuaJIT 2.0 (5.1), so `BENCH:Yield()` errored on *every* call. Since `Benchmark` yields between runs, this broke the entire measuring path in-game — a full `internet_benchmark_run` would have failed immediately on a real server. Now uses `coroutine.running()`, which is correct on 5.1 and later.
- **`WriteAsset` didn't create its output directory**, relying on a side effect of `HTMLReport` having run first. GMod's `file.Write` fails *silently* when the directory is missing, so calling it standalone quietly wrote nothing. All writes now go through a shared `BENCH:WriteOutput`.
- **`ReadSource` left a carriage return on every line** of a CRLF-saved file, corrupting sources in reports generated on Windows servers.
- Zero-valued results crashed the formatter on a nil prefix concat; percentages produced `nan%` against a zero minimum mean.
- `Title()` left the extension's dot behind; the standard prefix list was missing `10^24`.
- `Force*` log variants double-printed with a stray `true`; `Parse()` couldn't clamp to `NONE`.

### Architecture

Five nested per-layer coroutine pumps collapsed into a single yield-through design driven by one tick-budgeted `Async` pump. Resume errors now propagate with a traceback instead of being silently swallowed as results, and a faulted job clears its state so a crash can't wedge the suite until a map change.

### All 17 trials

The 15 missing trials are ported to the `TRIAL` builder. Render trials are gated `:If(CLIENT)` (v1 errored on include serverside, where `surface`/`draw`/`cam` don't exist); `ns_accessors` now probes for its gamemode's globals instead of erroring everywhere; helper functions that leaked as globals are local; colliding tab orders are unique.

### Entry points

`internet_benchmark_run`, `internet_benchmark_trial <name>` (with autocomplete) and `internet_benchmark_environment`, superadmin/console-gated serverside. Previously the only way in was `lua_run INTERNET_BENCHMARK:HTMLReport()`, documented nowhere.

### Methodology and environment statement

Every report now ships an `environment.txt` recording everything plain GLua exposes (realm, hosting mode, OS family, branch, game version, LuaJIT version/arch, JIT state, map, tickrate, players). The README states plainly what **cannot** come from plain GLua and needs a binary module or manual recording.

When the optional [gm_sysinfo](https://github.com/JoshPiper/gm_sysinfo) 3.x module is installed, the suite detects it and extends the statement with the precise OS version, kernel, distribution, CPU architecture, physical cores, memory/swap totals, 1/5/15-minute load averages and uptime — the load averages answering the "concurrent load" caveat the statement previously could only disclaim. Every getter is `pcall`-guarded (they raise rather than return nil, and future versions may change the surface), absence changes nothing, and the host name is deliberately never collected since these statements are meant to be published. CPU model/clock (not yet exposed by the module) and GPU remain manual.

CI installs the released **v3.0.1** binaries (checksum-pinned against the release's `SHA256SUMS`) into the test server, so the integration is verified against the real module in a live server, not just injected fakes — the real-binary case asserts the actual rows it produces.

### Tests, linting, CI, packaging

Two tiers, both in CI:

| Tier | Location | Covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | `tests/` | Statistics and formatting maths under stock LuaJIT via a GMod shim. No game needed. |
| Integration | `lua/tests/internet_benchmark/` | 56 [GLuaTest](https://github.com/CFC-Servers/GLuaTest) cases in a real GMod server: trial discovery and realm gating, introspection, the timing loop, the background pump, report rendering, file output, console commands, and the gm_sysinfo integration (via an injected fake module). |

Plus glualint, a README documenting methodology and its microbenchmark caveats, MIT `LICENSE`, and an `addon.json` that keeps repo-only files out of the packed addon.

## Verification

All three CI jobs green:

- **GLua Lint** — glualint 1.29.0, clean
- **Unit Tests** — 63 assertions under LuaJIT
- **In-Game Tests** — 56/56 GLuaTest cases passing in a real Garry's Mod server, including the environment integration exercised against the released gm_sysinfo v3.0.1 binary

Locally in addition: 42 files parse under LuaJIT, and full report generation driven end-to-end through the real `Async` pump (17 trials discovered, 13 run, 4 correctly gated, 12/12 structural checks).

### The first CI run failed, and that was the point

Running GLuaTest in a real server immediately caught the two bugs listed above — `coroutine.isyieldable` and the missing `file.CreateDir` — with 8 failing cases. Both were invisible locally because the shims were *more forgiving than the game*: the local interpreter is LuaJIT 2.1 (which has `isyieldable`), and the simulation created parent directories on write. Both shims were tightened to model the game's actual behaviour, and both bugs have regression coverage in the fast tier.

Two further CI bugs were caught before that, by running the tools by hand rather than trusting the workflow: the lint job downloaded the **aarch64** glualint asset (wrong architecture for the runner), and glualint exited 123 on `string_templating.lua`'s mixed quote styles. The quote change leaves the string literals byte-identical, so the benchmark measures exactly what it did before.

## Still worth doing before release

A manual `internet_benchmark_run` on a live server: CI proves the code paths work, but not that the *numbers* are sane. The client-only render trials (`draw_rect`, `set_draw_color`) can't be integration-tested headlessly at all — GLuaTest runs serverside, so they're only covered as correctly skipped.

## Follow-ups

- The report pulls Bootstrap, highlight.js, jQuery 2.1.3 (2014) and CanvasJS from CDNs. **CanvasJS is commercially licensed** — worth confirming that's acceptable, or swapping for a self-contained alternative.
- ~~Wire up `gm_sysinfo`~~ — done; the environment statement now uses it when installed. When gm_sysinfo grows CPU model/clock getters, two more rows in `sh_environment.lua` finish the hardware picture.

items.title: docs(claude): correct the module count and index already-built capabilities
items.body:
## What was wrong

`CLAUDE.md` said **"34 Rust modules"** and listed 34. `crates/core/src` contains **82**. The map covered 41% of the engine while presenting itself as complete.

Undocumented modules include `policy_fs.rs` (4,487 lines), `bounded_child.rs` (3,030), `search_index.rs` (2,039), `macos_graph_xpc.rs` (2,003), `autoresearch.rs` (1,688), `name_correction.rs` (968) and `vocabulary.rs` (811).

## Why it matters

"vocabulary" appears **zero times** in `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `README.md` and `PLAN.md`. It is documented under `docs/`, but not in any file an agent or new contributor reads to orient.

The consequence is concrete and repeated: the custom-vocabulary feature, the decode-hint biasing it feeds (`build_decode_hints` → `whisper_initial_prompt` → `set_initial_prompt`), and the hint-evaluation harness with `max_wer_regression` and required/forbidden term scoring have each been proposed as new work while already shipping. That is wasted effort at best and a duplicate implementation at worst.

## Change

- Corrects the count to 82 and marks the tree explicitly as a partial map, with the command to get the real list.
- Adds an **"Already Built — check here before proposing to build it"** table covering vocabulary, decode-hint biasing, the eval harnesses, the sherpa engine, name correction, and the large infrastructure modules, each with a way to verify it is live.
- Records two traps that produced wrong conclusions in practice:
  - `minutes transcribe` calls `DecodeHints::default()`, so it gets no vocabulary biasing; only the pipeline path does. Benchmarking name accuracy through `transcribe` measures the unbiased path.
  - `effective_batch_engine` reads as a silent engine swap until you read its caller, which warns.

Docs only. No behavior change.

## Decision

Add one current-state system architecture map that separates the governed repository system from executable programs/runtime, the broader framework, documentation, datasets/evidence artifacts, and governance.

Related to #1586.

## Scope

Documentation only. No runtime, schema, simulator, CI, governance contract, dataset, deployment, or roadmap behavior changes.

## Files changed

- `docs/architecture/system_architecture_map.md`
- `docs/README.md`
- `docs/context/AI_HANDOFF.md`

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Separates system, runtime/programs, framework, documentation, datasets/evidence, and governance.
- [x] Anchors scenario runtime claims to `runtime_contract.md`, applicable source, schemas, and tests.
- [x] Records `STATUS.md` and `v1_core/languages/es/` as the canonical v1 methodology relationship.
- [x] States that a reviewed Issue or PR does not govern by itself; only an applicable decision or ratification record supplies governance traceability.
- [x] Makes explicit that framework prose, RFCs, governance documents, datasets, drafts, and synthetic outputs do not become executable or verified capabilities through file presence.

Documentation-only. The map can become stale when repository capabilities change. Hosted Link Check and GitHub Mermaid rendering remain required. No deployment, professional-review, security, legal, or external-state attestation is made.

Independent review corrected an earlier authority overstatement and tightened the exact simulator, Operator, dataset-schema, and laboratory boundaries before publication.

Updated because #1586 resolves an architecture ambiguity and establishes a persistent contributor handoff boundary. The handoff preserves all existing runtime, authority, evidence, and non-capability limits.

Handle #1587 separately after this PR merges: add the short normative glossary for system/program/runtime/framework without rewriting this map or existing implementation contracts.

items.title: docs: fix inaccurate readme claims and document bundle size
items.body:
Verified every claim against the published `phosphor-react-native@3.0.6`, the `react-native-svg` source, and `tsc --strict --skipLibCheck false`.

## Tree-shaking claim (closes the README part of #61)

The README promised "Phosphor supports tree-shaking, so your bundle only includes code for the icons you use". Metro does not tree-shake by default, and the benchmark from #88 shows the barrel import costs +182% vs +10% for a direct import. Replaced with a **Bundle size** section carrying those numbers, plus the two real fixes: direct imports, or Expo's experimental tree-shaking.

## Fixes

- **Deep import path.** `phosphor-react-native/lib/commonjs/icons/Star` is not in the `exports` map — it fails with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED` on any resolver honouring `exports`, which Metro does by default since RN 0.79. Removed; documented `src/icons/*` and its naming rule.
- **TypeScript snippet did not compile.** `interface SvgProps extends DefaultSvgProps` is self-recursive (`TS2310`) and `DefaultIconProps` was never imported (`TS2304`). Rewritten as plain module augmentation, with a note on why `extends` is wrong. Same bug fixed in `global.d.ts`.
- **Props.** Dropped "accepts all SVG props, including `onClick`" — `IconProps` is closed and RN has no `onClick`. Corrected the size-unit list: `react-native-svg` runs `parseInt`, so `"2rem"` is 2, not 32. Corrected `duotoneColor`, which falls back to `color`, not black. Added the missing `style` prop and per-prop defaults.
- **Migrating from v2.** Documents the `Icon` suffix, and that `Circle` / `Path` / `Infinity` have no deprecated alias (1509 of 1512 do).

items.title: docs: v0.4 documentation and re-measured benchmarks
items.body:
Final PR of v0.4: documentation, a measured optimisation, and a full benchmark
re-run.

## The optimisation came out of writing the benchmark

`IncrBy` read the clock unconditionally. It never computes a new deadline — it
judges liveness and copies the one the key already has — so it can use `readNow`,
which returns the zero time when no key in the store carries an expiry at all.

**151 ns → 102 ns.** The benchmark with a deadline present is unchanged at 180
ns, which is the check that the clock is what moved rather than the map lookup.
This is v0.2's finding again, where reading `time.Now` on every `GET` made the
read path five times slower than v0.1 for a store that might hold no TTLs.

## Two findings from re-measuring, both of which say something

**A measurement error caught before publication.** The first end-to-end pass ran
Redis with `--daemonize yes`. That instance answered a single-connection `GET`
benchmark at **10 035 rps, p50 0.095 ms**, against our 35 236 rps at 0.023 ms —
a result that would have let `docs/benchmarks.md` claim we are three times faster
than Redis. The same Redis build started in the foreground answers **35 971 rps
at 0.023 ms**. The finding was about how the oracle was launched. It is written
into the file because the wrong number was the flattering one, which is exactly
when a measurement gets published without a second look.

**The `everysec` cost is noisier than v0.3.0 reported.** Four interleaved pairs
give deltas of +3%, −7%, −18%, −8% — a median around 7%, but a spread that will
not support the 16% v0.3.0 quoted to two significant figures. The file now says
so, rather than replacing one tidy number with another.

Corrected figures, medians of three runs with both servers in the foreground,
one at a time: at 50 connections we reach 83–86% of Redis; at one connection we
are within 3%. Throughput is flat-to-declining across `GOMAXPROCS` 1→10, which
is the table that settles the sharding question.

## Documentation

- `docs/protocol.md`: the three commands, the `overflow` error class, and a
  counters section stating that the incrementable-value grammar is narrower than
  Go's `ParseInt` and which four forms that rules out
- `docs/architecture.md`: why `INCR` reads an absolute deadline rather than
  rebuilding one from the time remaining; why the generated-sequence recovery
  check runs after every step
- `README.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`
- Also corrected a contradiction that predates this PR: the parallel-reads
  section still said the lock's share of a real request "remains unmeasured"
  while the section above it contained the measurement

## Live verification on a real binary

```
SET c 5 EX 100 ; INCR c → 6 ; TTL c → 100
SIGTERM → clean drain → restart → recovered records=6
GET c → 6 ; TTL c → 84        (the same deadline, not refreshed)
GET big → 9223372036854775807 (unchanged by the refused INCR)
GET z   → 07                  (unchanged by the refused INCR)
```

That transcript is the milestone: the counter survived the restart carrying the
expiry it had, which is the failure ADR-0004 exists to prevent.

## Verification

`gofmt -l`, `go vet`, `staticcheck`, `go test -race ./...` clean; conformance
green against Redis 8.10.0 with and without `KV_AOF=1`.

items.title: feat(parallelism): parallel map-reduce & merge sort with speedup benchmarks (phase 4)
items.body:
## Phase 4 — Real parallelism & speedup

Moves from *concurrency* (structuring work) to *parallelism* (using cores) — and **measures** the speedup instead of assuming it.

| Package | API | Idea |
|---------|-----|------|
| `patterns/mapreduce` | `MapReduce[In,Out]` | chunked parallel map-reduce; associative reducer + identity |
| `patterns/psort` | `Sort[T]` | fork-join parallel merge sort (depth-bounded, sequential cutoff, stable) |

### Measured speedup (10 cores)
Two CLI demos print live speedup + `GOMAXPROCS`:

```
$ go run ./cmd/demo mapreduce --n 200000   ->  serial ~27ms / parallel ~5ms  =>  ~5x   (compute-bound)
$ go run ./cmd/demo psort --n 2000000      ->  stdlib ~134ms / parallel ~94ms =>  ~1.4x (bandwidth-bound)
```

The contrast is the lesson: **not all parallelism is equal** — map-reduce is compute-bound and scales well; sorting is memory-bandwidth bound, so Amdahl's law caps it far below the core count.

### Quality
- **100% coverage** on both packages; every test under **`-race` + `goleak`**.
- Serial-vs-parallel **benchmark pair** per package (`go test -bench .`).
- **Code-review pass**: verified the psort goroutines write to disjoint regions of both the slice and the shared scratch buffer (race-free), the fork-join joins before returning (no leak), the merge is correct and stable, and the mapreduce chunking/partials are race-free and order-preserving. No issues found.
- Found & handled a genuine subtlety: floating-point addition isn't associative, so the mapreduce demo compares serial vs parallel with a **relative** tolerance (documented as a parallel-reduction lesson).
- `gofmt`/`vet`/`golangci-lint` clean.

### Docs
- New **[docs/parallelism.md](docs/parallelism.md)**: Amdahl's law, fork-join & map-reduce Mermaid diagrams (validated), how to benchmark speedup, and when parallelism helps vs hurts. Fulfils the forward reference left in `scheduler.md`.
- Updated docs index and README contents/roadmap/demos.

Phase 4 of 5. Next: mini-applications combining the patterns.

items.title: benchmark/: a reproducible two-leg suite, and honest numbers in README
items.body:
The cross-implementation comparison was spike-frozen (S22/S23/S24) and hand-run. This promotes it to a committed, push-button harness and corrects two claims the fresh run does not reproduce.

## `benchmark/` (new)

- **`programs/`** — let-go's 7 benchmark files, vendored unmodified so the suite is self-contained (no dependency on the gitignored `references/` clones).
- **`run.sh`** — builds cljgo @HEAD, precompiles AOT binaries, auto-detects let-go (`$LETGO` or a reference clone), babashka, joker, clj. hyperfine 3 warmup / 10 runs, renders `results.md`. Artifacts to `.build/` (gitignored).
- **`README.md`** — methodology, binary/file sizes, **how an AOT binary is created**, and the `reduce` gap analysis.

## Two cljgo legs, not one

cljgo is a compiler, so a single column lies in either direction. `cljgo run` (interpreter) and `cljgo build` (AOT) are now reported side by side — mirroring how let-go publishes its VM against its own AOT. The compile speedup (~9–10× on user code) is visible rather than asserted.

| Benchmark | cljgo run | cljgo | let-go | babashka | joker | clojure JVM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| startup | 32.6 ms | 6.5 ms | **5.7 ms** | 12.5 ms | 9.1 ms | 338.0 ms |
| `tak` | 12.10 s | 858.5 ms | 1.38 s | 1.18 s | — | **531.8 ms** |
| `fib` | 9.32 s | 975.4 ms | 1.29 s | 1.16 s | — | **438.5 ms** |
| `loop-recur` | 482.3 ms | 52.1 ms | 49.8 ms | **45.5 ms** | 447.3 ms | 462.0 ms |
| `persistent-map` | 43.6 ms | **14.6 ms** | 15.7 ms | 18.9 ms | 34.8 ms | 449.1 ms |
| `map-filter` | 32.1 ms | 7.2 ms | **5.6 ms** | 10.5 ms | 9.9 ms | 340.4 ms |
| `transducers` | 88.5 ms | 20.9 ms | 26.7 ms | **16.2 ms** | — | 381.2 ms |
| `reduce` | 97.5 ms | 60.8 ms | 25.4 ms | **22.1 ms** | 1.56 s | 355.2 ms |

## Honest corrections (re-measured 2026-07-22, same machine)

- **`map-filter` is not an outright win.** This run: let-go 5.6 ms vs cljgo 7.2 ms. The 07-17 run had it 5.6 vs 6.3 the other way. Recorded as a tie, not a win.
- **Tool binary is 12 MB stripped, not 8.3 MB** — grew with keel, `cljgo new` templates, and `pkg/coreaot`. A compiled *program* is still 4.6 MB, and 12 MB is still the smallest runtime in the field.
- **`reduce` restated** at 2.4× let-go / 2.8× babashka (was 1.3× / 2.5×).

## Why `reduce` is the worst row

Documented rather than hand-waved. The fold loop is *already* native Go (ADR 0045), so `cljgo build` cannot rescue it — the cost is inside the loop at `lang.Apply2(f, acc, s.First())`: megamorphic `IFn` dispatch, every intermediate `long` boxed as `any`, and a seq node per step. `fib` wins for the mirror reason — its `(+ a b)` compiles to a direct `rt.Add` intrinsic, which a runtime-value reducing fn can never reach.

Fix path (Clojure-canonical, left to an ADR 0045 continuation): `IReduce`/internal-reduce on `range`/vectors, then native `map`/`filter`/`take`, then `Apply2` fast paths.

## Gates

`go build ./... && go vet ./... && gofmt -l ... && go test ./...` — all green.

items.title: Add full device-resident CUDA FMM backend (CudaFull) and CudaPartial alias
items.body:
### Motivation

- Provide a complete device-resident CUDA execution path so repeated FMM evaluations upload only moments and download only the final user-ordered field. 
- Reuse CPU-built static operators (P2M/M2M/M2L/L2L/L2P/P2P) by uploading them once and applying them on-device in dependency order without re-evaluating geometric formulas on the GPU. 
- Preserve and clearly expose the existing hybrid GPU path as a partial CUDA backend while adding explicit transfer/timing diagnostics and tests for the transfer contract. 

### Description

- Added new execution backend names `CudaPartial` (alias for the existing hybrid `CudaM2LP2P`) and `CudaFull` to `ExecutionBackend` and exposed them in the Python bindings. 
- Introduced a persistent full-device plan `CudaFullPlan` and supporting POD `CudaFullPlanData` and `CudaStaticLevel` carrying CPU-precomputed static operators, permutations, and the static P2P tensor; these are uploaded once and remain device-resident. 
- Implemented device kernels and orchestration to perform the repeated evaluation pipeline entirely on GPU for `CudaFull`: host H2D of moments + device permutation, `P2M`, level-ordered `M2M`, `M2L` (reused), level-ordered `L2L`, `L2P` (field-only), device `P2P`, accumulation + user-ordering, and one final D2H of fields. No multipoles/locals/matrices/tree data cross PCIe during normal repeated runs. 
- Kept CPU-side geometry/operator construction unchanged and added `build_cuda_full_plan()` to flatten CPU static operators into staged device entries; `UniformFmm::evaluate_into()` routes `CudaFull` field-only evaluations through the `CudaFullPlan`. 
- Added persistent device allocation, pinned staging buffers, identity-map enforcement (first-call fixed identity), detailed per-phase CUDA-event timings, and transfer/plan statistics (`CudaPlanStatistics` and `CudaEvaluationTimings`) extended to cover P2M/M2M/L2L/L2P/P2P/accumulation phases. 
- Integrated the backend into benchmarks and docs: benchmark selection accepts `cuda-partial` and `cuda-full`, README/roadmap/installation/validation updated to document behaviour and transfer contract, and Python bindings expose `CUDA_PARTIAL` and `CUDA_FULL`. 
- Added unit-level manual CUDA tests that validate numerical agreement and explicitly check the transfer contract (one moments-only H2D and one final-field-only D2H per repeated evaluation) and unchanged static/geometry upload counts across repeated evaluations. 

### Testing

- Built core library (CPU-only): `cmake -S . -B build-core -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCDFMM_BUILD_TESTS=OFF -DCDFMM_BUILD_PYTHON=OFF -DCDFMM_BUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF` and `cmake --build build-core -j2`; build succeeded. 
- Built benchmarks: `cmake -S . -B build-bench -DCDFMM_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON && cmake --build build-bench -j2`; build succeeded and benchmark executables were produced. 
- Ran `git diff --check` and local code checks; no issues reported. 
- Attempted full test build with tests and Python enabled but the Catch2 fetch step failed in this network-restricted environment (HTTP 403), blocking `cmake` test configuration; therefore full C++ test execution that depends on remote FetchContent could not complete. 
- Ran Python test collection for the benchmark runner but collection failed because `matplotlib` is not present in this environment, so Python test execution was not completed here. 
- CUDA runtime tests (device execution and full `CudaFull` correctness/transfer assertions) were not run in this environment because `nvcc`/CUDA toolkit or a CUDA-capable device was unavailable; per project policy these CUDA correctness/performance tests are manual and must be run on real CUDA hardware. 

If you want, I can: add more defensive checks around identity-map changes, factor per-stage memory layout for improved kernel performance, or prepare a small HOWTO for running the manual CUDA validation and benchmark suite on a CUDA host.

------

items.title: Calibrate benchmarks against Library Checker problems
items.body:
## Summary

Completely redesigned the benchmark suite to predict real-world performance by using actual Library Checker problems as workloads, rather than synthetic query mixes. This addresses systematic disagreements between benchmark results and judge performance.

## Key Changes

- **Workload redesign**: Replaced synthetic benchmarks with transcriptions of actual Library Checker problems:
  - `point_add_range_sum` (fenwicktree) - Point Add Range Sum problem
  - `staticrmq` (segtree) - Static RMQ problem  
  - `point_set_range_composite` (segtree) - Point Set Range Composite problem
  - `range_affine_range_sum` (lazysegtree) - Range Affine Range Sum problem
  - `unionfind` (dsu) - Unionfind problem
  - `scc` (scc) - Strongly Connected Components problem
  - `two_sat` (two_sat) - 2 SAT problem
  - `bipartitematching` (maxflow) - Matching on Bipartite Graph problem
  - `assignment` (mincostflow) - Assignment problem
  - Plus polynomial, string, and number theory workloads from Library Checker

- **Scaling system**: Introduced `ACL_BENCH_SCALE` environment variable and per-workload `COST_FACTOR` to normalize runtime across different problem complexities while staying within CI budgets. Each workload targets 1-4 seconds at default 0.2 scale.

- **Improved comparison logic** (`compare.py`):
  - Support for multiple time measurement files (interleaved passes for better noise estimation)
  - Uses minimum time across passes (not mean) to filter out CI runner interference
  - Noise-aware delta reporting: only flags changes larger than observed run-to-run variation
  - Minimum significance threshold (3%) to avoid reporting noise as improvements
  - Links benchmark names to their Library Checker problems

- **Comprehensive test coverage** (`test_benchmark_workloads.py`, `test_benchmark_compare.py`):
  - Correctness tests for all workload implementations against naive references
  - Tests for comparison report thresholds and noise handling
  - Validates that benchmarks actually solve the problems they claim to

- **Documentation**: Added extensive docstrings explaining why each design choice matters for predictive accuracy, plus `benchmarks/README.md` with problem mappings and historical context.

- **CI workflow updates** (`benchmark.yml`):
  - Interleaved base/PR measurement passes for better noise characterization
  - Environment variables for scale and round configuration
  - Increased timeout to 90 minutes for full-scale runs

## Notable Implementation Details

- **`_uniform_pair()`**: Implements Library Checker's `Random::uniform_pair` distribution for query ranges, which produces mean width of ~n/3 (more realistic than uniform random).

- **Workload class**: Unified interface with metadata (problem URL, full_size, effective_scale) while maintaining backward compatibility with existing `(name, build, run)` tuple consumers.

- **Operator realism**: Benchmarks use actual Python operators (e.g., affine map composition in Point Set Range Composite) rather than C builtins, so overhead measurements match real submissions.

- **Answer accumulation**: All `run_*` functions accumulate results rather than discarding them, matching how real submissions work and preventing dead-code elimination.

- **Noise estimation**: `spread()` function measures relative variation between passes to set per-benchmark significance thresholds, preventing false positives from CI runner variance.

items.title: Research: map CM1 terrain and the dry mountain-wave benchmark
items.body:
Closes #401 when PM approval and merge posture are satisfied.

Parent decision log: #400

## Scope

Creates exactly one research artifact:

`docs/research/mountain-waves/cm1-terrain-and-dry-benchmark-mapping.md`

This is desk research only. It does not run CM1 or implement terrain, moisture, a World, Recipe, Control, Lens, Comparison, scenario, route, or generic terrain framework.

## Primary evidence

- CM1 r21.1 tag `21.1` at official commit `0f734f64efa89a684963a66d2ac32db67617912b`
- Tag-pinned `src/init_terrain.F`, `src/base.F`, `src/input.F`, `src/param.F`, `src/bc.F`, `src/writeout.F`, and `src/writeout_nc.F`
- Tag-pinned `run/config_files/nh_mountain_waves/namelist.input`, `README.terrain`, and `README.namelist`
- CM1 governing equations
- Gal-Chen and Somerville (1975), Durran and Klemp (1983), Klemp et al. (2003), and Doernbrack et al. (2005)
- Current Cloud Chamber package, staging, manifest, ingest, output-product, visualization, and Three.js code

## Configured CM1 provenance used

Repository-recorded prior verification identifies:

- release: CM1 21.1
- official source commit: `0f734f64efa89a684963a66d2ac32db67617912b`
- source-manifest SHA-256: `fbe2367dfcd6d8c55cac4bd03362d8d49f13f80cebd13b36230c20d71119a84e`
- executable SHA-256: `5b7304bb04514ec03cf4d6e604bc0b5df6e8076bd4fb53c4b5cf5ea9184cdfd1`
- configured `README.namelist` SHA-256: `7b95be56db51f5c9396c59dca252cf96b918a312cc70107451f91149a34ab3b5`

This issue did not rehash Tim's configured local files.

## Principal findings

- r21.1 terrain is a scalar-grid `zs(x,y)` field. Built-in `itern=1-3` shapes and parameters are source-defined; `itern=4` reads one x-fastest, y-next, four-byte-real direct-access record from `perts.dat` on rank 0 and broadcasts it.
- The official case uses the Gal-Chen/Somerville transform. Its lower boundary is terrain-tangent, so Cartesian `w = u dzs/dx + v dzs/dy`, not `w=0`; `bbc=1` is free slip with no surface drag or heat/moisture flux.
- The bundled case is 2-D, dry, 100 x 1 x 100 at 200 m, with a 400 m / 1 km bell ridge, `N=0.01 s^-1`, `u=10 m/s`, and a 2,160 s duration.
- With `stretch_z=0`, active `maxz` is 20 km even though the inert namelist contains `ztop=18 km`; r21.1 NetCDF writes that inert scalar, so evaluation must use startup `maxz` or the top nominal `zf` level.
- Native terrain NetCDF has 1-D nominal `zh`/`zf`, 2-D `zs`, and 3-D scalar-level physical height `zhval`; physical full-level heights for `w` must be reconstructed and verified.

## Official dry-case mapping result

The official configuration is mapped setting by setting with each material value classified as a direct official benchmark setting, CM1 implementation default, operational/output choice, or execution-required verification. No official pointwise reference field or numeric tolerance was found, so the later gate uses exact configuration invariants plus structural, integrity, boundary, and damping evidence without inventing thresholds.

## Current Cloud Chamber compatibility and gaps

- Generic package rendering hard-codes flat terrain and cannot emit the case; a dedicated bounded generator is required.
- The built-in case consumes no `LANDUSE.TBL`, `perts.dat`, external grid, or external sounding.
- Current output ingest only recognizes `cm1out_######.nc`; the official GrADS files and single `cm1out.nc` do not match.
- Ingest retains `zs`/`zhval` metadata in a matching NetCDF sequence, but the field catalog and browser payloads do not interpret terrain.
- Existing slices, profiles, time-height products, point clouds, and Three.js placement use one-dimensional vertical coordinates and would misplace native terrain-following fields.

## Proposed later dry gate

One test-covered dedicated package, one official-duration run, output-only conversion to per-time NetCDF, and direct terrain-aware native-NetCDF evaluation. No CM1 smoke process, rerun, correction, moisture extension, or product implementation is authorized without explicit PM approval.

## Disposition

`advance_to_dry_reproduction`

This does not establish successful execution, quantitative benchmark validation, terrain-aware UI, a moist case, or product approval.

## Execution-only unresolved questions

- Does the configured executable terminate normally with the exact case and NetCDF output change?
- Are all required fields finite, correctly staggered, and present at every expected time?
- Does central-domain wave structure remain interpretable without material lateral/top reflection or damping contamination?
- Do the Coriolis and large-scale pressure-gradient tendencies leave the intended base flow acceptably balanced?
- Does actual output confirm the documented 18 km `ztop` metadata versus 20 km active-top discrepancy?

## Verification

- `git diff --name-only main...HEAD` -> exactly the approved research artifact
- `git diff --check` -> passed
- `scripts/check.sh` -> passed: 119 frontend tests, production build, 558 backend tests, script syntax, forbidden-artifact, and docs/JSON/YAML checks
- `git status --short` -> clean

## Confirmations

- No CM1 process ran.
- No generated package, runtime artifact, source copy, PDF, or screenshot was committed.
- No product concept or moist case was approved.
- No later issue was created.
- Manual review is required.
- Auto-merge is disabled.

items.title: feat(#45): per-node adjacency map + benchmark harness

Closes #45.

## What & why
Fetching a node's outgoing edges previously meant scanning the whole edge array (`O(m)` per lookup). This adds a per-node adjacency index so lookups are `O(1)` — the inner-loop primitive every BMSSP stage (BaseCase #40, FindPivots #44, main recursion #43) needs to relax edges.

### `src/bmssp.mjs`
- `this.adjacency: Map<nodeId, Array<[to, weight]>>` built in the constructor (every known node gets an entry; sinks get `[]`).
- `buildAdjacency()` — (re)builds the map from `this.graph`.
- `getEdges(nodeId)` — O(1) lookup, `[]` for unknown nodes.

### Tests
5 new unit tests (edge grouping, sink handling, one-entry-per-node, edge-count preservation on `roadNet-CA`, `getEdges`). **12/12 pass, 100% coverage on `bmssp.mjs`.** The existing BMSSP-vs-Dijkstra equivalence test still passes.

### Benchmarks (`benchmarks/`, `npm run bench`)
- Seeded, deterministic graph generators: sparse-random, dense-random, grid, chain, star.
